doc_text:
the bad news is that i now have a $7,000.00 dog.  the good news is that i have a $7,000.00 relatively healthy dog.

lucy presented in kidney failure (long story--regular vet problem) with bun and creatinine off the charts.  lucy's body temp was 91.1 f, and she was extremely lethargic.  

staff--all of them--were thoroughly professional and compassionate.  lucy was in critical care for a week; was returned for an additional five days three days after original release.  had nasogastric feeding tube initally; replaced by esophageal tube on second admission.  first admit was spent under heat tent.  daily kidney values.   

during both admissions, a vet called me every morning with a progress note.  because of transportation problems, i was unable to visit daily.  when they called, they were able to describe exactly where she was physically and were able to answer all of my questions.  i felt that lucy was getting individual care from vets and vet techs/nurses.  

when lucy was discharged, she was provided with a good supply of liquid diet for use with her feeding tube, and six cans of wet kidney diet dog food.  instructions for tube feeding were provided.

i took lucy to see my regular vet for follow-up yesterday and she's doing much better than expected.  her bun is normal and her creatinine is barely above the normal range.  she's eating and she's gained 0.3 lb. (which is pretty good for an 8-pound dog.)  her behavior is almost back to normal, which i feel is very good for a dog who was practically dead a month ago.

yes, med vet is expensive, but my furbaby got excellent care and, when you consider that she was in critical care for 11 days, the cost isn't totally unreasonable.  i feel she got excellent, life-saving care from a thoroughly professional, competent, and compassionate staff.  everyone, including the receptionists, was concerned about lucy and me.  

the only reason i gave a four-star rating instead of five is because i think her original release was too early and that she should have been  kept a couple of days longer, which would have eliminated the second admission.

it'll take me a long time to pay my credit card down, but i have a happy, relatively healthy dog because of it.  she'll be on a special diet for the rest of her life but, with reasonable care, she should have a normal lifespan.

the issue has not been resolved as of this review.

i have a trained service dog for mobility and medical alert. while my disabilities can be invisible, it's usually not as you can see i have a major walking issue. i worked with a local service dog training organization that meets assistance dogs international standards to get him. he is legit, no amazon certificate or anything. he took 2 years of training and cost tens of thousands to train.

his mobility vest is made of leather. it doesn't fit currently (we think it shrank due to rain and not having proper care taken of it) and we're waiting on his new one to come in (takes up to 8 weeks because it had to be custom made as it's a mobility/guide vest). still, he was leashed to his collar and had a couple leash wraps that showed he was a working service dog. we even put on his working booties (they're heavier duty than what you can get at petco and meant for working dogs). we have the laws printed out and highlighted and i/my boyfriend both know how to answer the required questions.

yesterday, i had three important doctors appointments. i've waited several weeks for them (about a month) and they were supposed to be a new step in figuring out my chronic disability. they were also about a 40 minute drive to get to them. between the first appointment and the second, i thought it would be a good idea to get a printout of my medical records, as my new school was requesting them.

sorry for the length  it's copied from the letter send to our congressman. 

   what can i say, this place raises my blood pressure like no other.  a few years ago i had issues with my father and the va which is a story in itself but i ended up talking to cong. ralph abraham. 3 years later i'm right back at the same spot. the community choice program was enacted approx  4-5 years ago to allow vets to see outside pcps & specialist when they live over 60 miles away. va not only wouldn't recommend this service but dissuaded vets by telling them their request wouldn't be approved. we bypassed that with help from cong.  abraham and for a couple years had no issues seeing outside drs. it was a nightmare to get the referrals and approvals but was doable if vigilant.  if a vet doesn't like his team dr( there are approximately 8 teams at this location) they can request a change. we request a team change in august of 2016, it took 13 months before he was changed. his only options were to continue to see the dr that he was unhappy with.   he would have to go to urgent care to be seen during this time had he not been on the cc program. they way it worked, you contacted triwest(whose in charge of referrals and approvals). if you don't get these prior approvals in hand it's likely they won't pay. they worked fairly quickly by va standards.  older vet wouldn't be able to get this done. after seeing outside drs we had multiple issues with the va team. despite telling the team dr and every nurse we encountered, do not change their medications or treatment without seeing the vet or consulting the cc pcp.  dr. kept changing medications and treatment without seeing the vets or consulting with cc pcp. the cc pcp had to call and change everything back.  this program also takes almost a year to pay so many drs don't want to mess with them. but after lots of work we got it done and it worked reasonably well for 2 years. 
   typical day at the va. we could no longer contact triwest to get referrals and their cc primary care dr could no longer request referrals to specialist or drs. we were told by triwest and va staff that from that point on to see an outside dr. the vet must drive to the alex va to see team dr to get a referral to see his pcp. no other way to see an  cc pcp.  have to wait wks/mths to see the team dr, must see va dr or specialist to get the referrals to an outside specialist. to be clear,  we drive over 65 miles, see 1 dr wait for appt with va specialist to refer to cc dr.   one vet had a diabetic ulceration on his foot that had reopened after a 16 months of extensive treatment, contacted his team dr, yellow team, dr santiago. to next available appt was 4 mnths.  advised to go to urgent care. cc is essentially useless now. at the last primary va appt, put in for the referrals to continue his care with his pcp and cardiologist but don't expect it to be approved. the rn said she  had never had a single request approved to see an outside dr, never.  we did get approval to continue to see their outside cardiologist, but no news on outside primary care.

i told him i couldn't breath to which he made us aware "we're not set up for that here" (even though we were in the emergency room) and "you're going to be here for a while".

we were blown away by the callousness of the response and momentarily considered going to another emergency room, but because i was having trouble breathing we decided to stay.

people have bad days, i get it. but when your job is to help people that are having the worst day of their life, a little compassion might be in order. you should never greet any person that is scared, or in pain with "you came to the wrong damn place". even if you personally can't help, it is incumbent on you as a decent human being to help get them help. this is especially true when your job is to "help" people.

with so much negativity in the media about various health care issues that it is easy to overlook those caregivers who do their best to provide the best possible care.

i have just finished six weeks of outpatient rehabilitation for a bi-lateral knee replacement at the rehab services department at broward health in coral springs. 
  
everything - from the warm and compassionate greeting from joanie who answered my initial, very  nervous call - to the sessions thrice, then twice, then single weekly sessions paul mcgowen have been noteworthy for his skill, compassion, encouragement  and knowledge of various physical therapeutic exercises.

understanding that i have made years of accommodations for my fused knees prior to my surgery, paul incorporated hip and lower back exercises into my pt plan.  he gave me exercises for home and followed up each session with a progress report.  he told me what to watch for - how to correct myself.  in short - he cared.

bhcs rehab consists of an incredible group of people - and for this, the program director, ms. pomerantz should be recognized.  she has put together an incredible team.  it was not unusual for any of the other therapists - edwin, amanda, allison and monica - to stop by me (either on the table or on a machine) to cheer me on.    youlanda was always ready provide heat and ice and tell me how great i was doing.

i have been to other facilities for physical therapy.  i know what it is to be treated as a case number.  i know what it is to be viewed as an insurance claim and nothing more.  this is not the case at broward health coral springs.  my experience with paul and his colleagues has completely "etch-a-sketched" those very negative experiences from my memory. 
 
my life has changed dramatically for the best - and i owe much of it to paul mcgowan and the rehab group at bhcs.  i thank them all.

hopefully you read this before going to the er, not after like i did.  reading some of the other reviews - similar things happened to me.

on friday february 28th at about 8:30pm my daughter and i took our 18 month old grandson to the emergency room on bee ridge and cattlemen.  

1.  my daughter was holding the baby who was crying - he had been bitten on the hand by a dog.
2.  the security guard never looked up from his computer and mumbled for us to sit down - "they know you're here."  we were the only people in the er, so i'm thinking "who knows we're here?"
3.  three women were behind a desk and did not make eye contact with us - no concern for a young woman holding a crying baby.  they just talked to each other - nobody told us anything.
4.  five minutes becomes 10 minutes and nobody said anything to us.
5.  after about 10-12 minutes a door marked triage opens and some patient comes out.  the triage nurse asked us to come in.
6.  she did not wash her hands, use purell, or wear gloves.
7.  she had to do all the typing to get us into the system (i guess the other three women were busy not helping)
8.  after about 15 questions - she finally asked why we were here.  we told her he had been bitten by a dog.
9.  when she reached for his hand - he of course screamed - so she reached for an unsanitized teddy bear on her desk and gave that to him to quiet him down.
10.  she dabbed the wound clean (did not rinse it) and moved us through some double doors into another waiting room with about six chairs - again we were the only people there.
11.  about another 10-15 minutes later a nurse came in and confirmed the baby's name.  then she asked us if he had a fever?  no?  a cough?  no?  we told her he had a dog bite.  (i wonder why she hadn't read the triage report??)
12.  she asked my daughter a dozen questions which had nothing to do with the dog bite, including vaginal or c-section delivery?  i'm guessing that is a priority when treating a dog bite.
13.  another 10 - 15 minutes and a doctor came into the room.  and here's where i started to question this whole operation.  he never came closer than 10 feet from the baby - never looked at the wound, let alone cleaned it.  from 10 feet away he then described what he was going to do - he was going to order an x-ray and then give us some antibiotics - because he told us without antibiotics the risk of infection is very high.
14.  another 10-15 minutes and a guy from x-ray came and told us he had been instructed to an x-ray of the right hand.  "is this _____?"  good guess!

did you ever see the movie zootpia where she has to go to the dmv to get her license?  that's what this experience brought to my mind.  they were like the sloths but without the smile and the compassion.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drhsktakrzc 

15.  another 30 minutes and the nurse came back asking us what was happening.  that is when i got a little frustrated and asked her why the doctor had not even looked at the wound?  why hadn't the wound been cleaned?  she seemed to think that the doctor had looked at the wound.
16.  i could go on and on...

finally the nurse came back with the prescription for the antibiotic - it was now 11 at night.  i asked her if she could call in the prescription so it would be ready when we got there.  "we don't provide that service."

this is a perfect example of an organization which is driven by procedure - and has absolutely no focus on patients.  no compassion, no coordination, no communication.  the system these people work in has crushed their humanity - and this is with an empty er.

all the while i'm thinking to myself - "omg imagine if there was a corona virus outbreak in sarasota and there were five or six puking sick people in the er waiting room?  this hospital is completely unprepared to handle anything like that."

come to find out two days later that there was a corona virus patient in the hospital that night - and i thought back to the people not washing their hands, etc. etc.  i pray that my grandson, my daughter and i were not infected.  

and hannah b. don't respond "i am so sorry to hear about your experience..."  if you gave a damn, you would go to the er yourself and see what your customers see - it isn't pretty.  if you did care, it would either be fixed, or you wouldn't be working there.

as an almost 25 year military veteran who's been fortunate enough to serve around the globe, and been in quite a few hospitals and medical facilities.  this hospital is by far the worst i've ever encountered! earlier this month, i had the misfortune of visiting this hospital's er during a medical emergency of severe pain in my shoulder, arm, and fingers.

now, i understand that there are basic protocols that have to be performed such as collecting name, address, identification, etc.  but between the lack of expediency, the rude dispositions, the dismissive attitudes, and the lack of actually trying to identify a problem, this "clinic" was an utter waste of time.

i had a "nurse" actually snatch a piece of paper from my hand when she realized i didn't care for her rudeness. that was not very professional nurse mary.  i was talked down to, condescended to, and ultimately sent home with a "you don't actually have an emergency" comment".

i'm on the road to recovery and i'm thankful to the doctors at penn medicine for taking my complaints seriously.  shame on abington - lansdale hospital!  i've reported my experience at this facility to hopefully prevent someone/anyone else from receiving the same horrendous treatment that i received. disgraceful! unsat!

doc_text:
i was the support person for my daughter's recent labor and delivery. the labor and delivery service was mostly good, but the time after the delivery was awful.
we came to the delivery room around midnight and my daughter delivered at 2:30 with an uncomplicated natural childbirth with no pain medication. the delivery was very smooth and the dr. was skilled and personable. i thought it was a wonderful delivery.

because i was my daughter's support person, i was there for the entire 31 hours after delivery. and this is my story. 

we got in the recovery room about 4 and the nurses began their protocol of patient care. my daughter was not allowed to sleep more than 2 hours at a time, plus she was caring and feeding her newborn. nurses continued to wake her up over and over for some sort of patient care, that was in my opinion mostly unnecessary. at one point a nurse came in to wake her up and ask her if she wanted a pain pill. where is the common sense in that?
i got her out of there as quick as possible because she needed rest after being exhausted by delivery. she guesses she got 3 hours of sleep in the 31 hours she was there after delivery. perhaps this is a way to get new mothers out as soon as possible?

the sad thing is many new parents don't realize how abusive this protocol is and just accept it as normal. even the lactation specialist i complained to said she had her baby at home for that exact reason. a natural, un-medicated delivery is a normal part of life. and in my opinion the hospital's patient care is abusive.

we all joke that new parents are sleep deprived, but in the hours after delivery a new mother should be allowed to sleep if baby will let them. i worry about other mothers who may have had complication. they need the rest more than anyone and i know they will be denied rest by hospital patient care. 

we asked to be left alone for a few hours for sleep. the staff agreed then just continued on with all the things they are required to do. 

we left a day early so my daughter could come home and get some rest and she has been doing that. she would have liked to stay the full time because she has another child to care for and she is a single mother, but she told me she was so exhausted, that she needed to leave. she said she couldn't keep her eyes open and i saw that every time her eyes closed she would immediately be asleep. how is a person that exhausted able to care for a newborn or even herself?

i'm sorry for anyone who delivers at a hospital especially this one.  patients are trusting your hospital with their health and a very very important part of health is rest.

for the insane cost of this "private" facility, you'll end up in a whole world of hurt. 

a close family member ("cc") was involved with this program for a little over 2.5 years. after "graduating," cc then relocated and continued in outpatient therapy with the same psychiatrist. a few months ago, we terminated treatment with this provider. we finally realized that the provider was squirrely at best and only sought to make messes for cc that he would have no part in cleaning up.

prior to entering treatment, cc was on zero medications, had zero hospitalization, and zero history of drug abuse. cc was in school full time, working part time, active in our church community, and generally managing. following a traumatic life event, we voluntarily chose to have cc enter the retreat on the recommendation of our home psychologist. 

after a series of: 
-tms (junk science), 
-ect (victorian, invasive shock therapy), 
-2 years worth of toxic medication trials, and 
-1.5 years of outpatient group therapy
-relocating cc several states away to continue treatment, 
we are at a massive loss emotionally and financially.

the retreat psychiatrist (who led our family member's care) had far too much faith in his own capabilities. he had a deceptively closed-minded focus on his personal field of study, which we know now, doesn't really help with the functional treatment of complex trauma. we didn't get to choose cc's providers, but knowing what we know now, we never would have chosen this path for them. 

you practically need a phd in psychiatric practice to understand how this program works. we were very blindsided to learn that the arcane psychoanalysis was the foundation for the retreat's programming. they tout dbt, but it's two sessions per week, which are confusing and disorganized at best. 

the treatment team routinely exercised poor judgement in assessing the dynamics of cc's complicated trauma background, which continued throughout the entire course of care. they essentially allowed cc's biological parents (and main payors) to dictate the care and treatment strategies used, which resulted in a series of misdiagnoses.

it's a rampant issue in healthcare, but the providers are wholly protected by the system from bearing any consequence for their "firm suggestions." they put the onus on the patients and their families to be the ultimate deciders, but it really became a toxic cycle of the blind leading the blind. we didn't feel like we had a choice at any point if we wanted cc to get on a path to recovery. 

think of sinking an average year's salary for a 3-week-long diagnostic workup by a supposed "team of experts." a mix of art therapists and social workers will work with your psychiatrist to strong arm the patient into a desire to "get better" and then coerce the family into refinancing their home to get the recommended weeks to months of extended care at over $2000 per day. this includes an intensive regimen of loosey-goosey therapy groups, bizarre binders full of self-help jargon, and patient-guided group therapy. they are trying to be progressive, but it's a classic case of poor administrative controls and defaulting into letting the inmates run the asylum. it honestly feels like some of the providers get a kick out making things messy and watching us drown while we try to clean up catastrophe after catastrophe. they just smile at us and placate us with politicized psychiatric jargon.

once we pursued outside consultation, we realized we'd been completely, wholly, massively duped by these supposed "experts" and gamed by a very unregulated rehabilitation system. unless medication management and positive talk therapy are the $200,000+ boost you need, these people constantly come up short.

after all is said and done, we were dealing with an entirely different medical and psychiatric picture than the providers were willing to treat or even investigate. hundreds of thousands of dollars later, and hundreds of hours of travel, family therapy, and the many years cc devoted to their own therapy, we have very little to show for it. 

we are left with immeasurable pain and suffering, a heap of debt, and a solid education in the toxic dysfunction of the behavioral health system.

thanks mountain view !
martin swartout

please, learn from my mistake. if you find yourself in an ambulance with an emt asking you which hospital to go to, under no circumstances say "king's county". say no to this place like your life depends on it. 

my particular horror story happened on a saturday morning when i began feeling a crippling, agonizing and debilitating pain in my abdomen, getting worse and worse. unable to move and barely able to stay conscious, i called 911 and an ambulance took me to the nearest hospital -- king's county. 

i was wheeled into the er on a gurney, crying and screaming in agony. after several minutes, someone asked for my insurance card. thinking that i was about to die, i cried and used profanity to plead for help. she said she didn't like my language and simply walked away.

i lay there, crying in agony and fearful that i was on death's door. i thrashed on my gurney, pleading for help. a full hour went by as i cried and pleaded for help, while the staff all around completely ignored me. i listened through my pain as they gossiped, engaged in long discussions about what they would have for lunch, and as they answered phones from people in distress and then joked about how "stupid" the callers were. after an hour a doctor happened to walk by. i reached out for him, pleading for help. he took one look at me and shouted at the staff that i should be a priority patient. 

i lay in the lobby for another 20 minutes, feet away from the open door in the middle of winter. 

finally i was wheeled into the hospital by a staff member who slammed my gurney into each and every door and wall, furthering the worst agony i had ever experienced. he ignored me, stopping to have a casual chat with another staffer about the upcoming super bowl. he then wheeled me into the middle of a busy hallway in the er, locked the wheels of the gurney, and left me there. for the next half hour, countless people bumped into me as my cries for help went unanswered. after vomiting several times, the pain became so unbearable that i lost consciousness. 

i woke up to a woman asking for my insurance again. i begged her for help, and she just walked away. 30 minutes later a friendly doctor (the only positive part of this experience) briefly examined me in the hallway (where privacy was nonexistent) and said they needed to run tests. after an endless wait, a horrendously mean nurse withdrew 5 vials of blood from my arm (i was later told this was a mistake and they only needed 2, so the others were disposed of). she hooked me up to an iv, left a bunch of literal garbage (wrappers and packaging from needles, etc) on top of me, and left. for 2 hours, no one would acknowledge my presence as i cried in pain. my questions went unanswered. it had been hours since i had anything to drink or gone to the bathroom, and with an empty iv bag connected to my arm, i was literally trapped on the bed, unable to move. 

i asked everyone who walked past (or rather, everyone who bumped into me) but i was ignored. occasionally, a nurse or staff member would walk by and treat me with about as much respect as they would give a stray animal. the staff here have no business dealing with patients, let alone other human beings. interacting with them was undoubtedly the single most dehumanizing experience of my entire life. 

after hours of this agony, of being ignored, of being literally denied the ability the use the bathroom or access to water, i told a staff member that i was on the verge of calling the police to report that i was being held captive against my will and tortured. this got their attention. the doctor came back, surprised that no one had spoken to me, surprised that i had been tied to this bed for so long, and very surprised that the nurse dumped her garbage on top of my lap. she ordered more tests and unhooked my iv. i waited 17 minutes to use the only available bathroom, peed into a cup, and held onto the urine for another 30 minutes until someone took it. after another endless wait, she came back to say she thought i had a kidney stone and suggesting i get a ct scan. well i finally got that scan, but they didn't bother to walk me back to my bed so i got lost, wandering the sprawling hospital halls... 

after a full day of being abused, abandoned, restrained, ignored, and borderline tortured, i wad diagnosed with a kidney stone, given a prescription to pick up from a pharmacy that had already closed, and sent on my way. look, no er is a fun place, and i understand that this one is working under exceptionally difficult circumstances out of their control. but there is simply no justification for what i experienced. i once visited a hospital in an impoverished, rural community in china, and the people there were treated with infinitely more respect and dignity. king's county er resembles a hospital from a post-apocalyptic zombie movie. but in a world without zombies, there is simply no excuse. shame on them. shame! you've been warned.

(how many gals who just graduated with a pa license from strayer online does it take to manage an er full of, say, 5-7 patients?  15-20, apparently.  three to four illustrious worker bees for each patient lucky enough to end up at this underwhelming facility - not a bad ratio, in theory, but practice falls short, believe you me.)  no bedside manner (the key, glaring deficiency), sparing smiles, more or less basic command of verbal communication but nothing to write home about.  thankfully the news was good, but we would have appreciated it a couple of hours earlier.  and, hey, i'm not a medical operations specialist or anything, but perhaps an emergency room operation can optimize efficiency and effectiveness by clearing easy cases out sooner rather than later?  disappointing experience.  we'll opt for gwu, sibley or the effing minute clinic at pentagon city mall the next time around.

intro
this review is a commentary on the staff and administrators at 
usmd/mcnt, not the doctors. all of the information contained in this review is verifiable. 
backstory
i was a patient of the mcnt practice for many years and had my annual physicals there many times over the past decade. the annual screening is used to discount my insurance costs. three years ago my screening form was "misplaced". last year i was told it was faxed however, they could not provide the transmission report. to ensure the form was submitted on time this year i planned to pick up the form and submit it myself.
current events 
when i arrived at the office for my appointment i explained my past problems with the screening form to the nurse (rachel) and the doctor (hyatt). they assured me the form would be completed and they would call me as soon as my blood test results were in and added the test results normally came in three days. since my appointment was on friday i contacted them twice on the following tuesday. i received no response. i called twice on wednesday. i did receive a  message from the nurse on wednesday afternoon reporting the test results were in and awaiting the doctor's signature. i called twice on thursday and once again on friday. i did not receive any responses to these messages. i arrived at the usmd office friday afternoon around 3 pm. i explained that i was upset at not having received a response to my numerous messages and that i needed my screening form that afternoon to meet the deadline. a short time later i was ushered into the vacant hematology lab by rachel and told my form had not been signed and that the doctor was on holiday. i was furious! i explained loudly but respectfully that i needed to leave the office with the form to meet the deadline and requested that another doctor sign the form. i was then told no doctor would be able to sign the form that day and that their responsibility did not include notifying me or completing the form. i responded that i would not leave without the signed form. i received the signed form around 4 pm. i left, commenting on their horrendous customer service and poor communication skills. on my way to fedex, i called the usmd administrative offices in irving, texas. i was greeted by a very polite administrative assistant. she patiently listened to my comments, explained that most of the senior staff was gone for the day but that someone would get back to me on monday. this was  november 22, 2019. i never received a call.
closing
as i noted in the introduction the doctors at this office are outstanding. fortunately, my gp left the practice so i do not need to find a new doctor. having said that i will only go back to this office to retrieve my medical records. the customer service is deplorable, some of the staff are incompetent and certainly shouldn't be working with people. the usmd offices are no better since they were "unable" to return my call. i would avoid any usmd offices, specifically the mcnt office in flower mound, texas.

i can't imagine any other business where you are spending thousands of dollars at an establishment and the people working there treat the clients like they are trash, and are annoyed with them for existing.

i met the doctor for the first time during my stay in the er when he burst into the room saying, "i'd like to know what possible reason you could have for holding up a ct scan!"  not, "hello, how are you feeling?" not, "hi i'm dr. gionis."  i'd been waiting literally hours to see him the middle of the night, after a day spent throwing up with a fever. it was 3am.  i deserved kindness and gentleness, not being attacked.  that is an incredibly rude way to treat anyone, period. second of all, when you're the doctor and a large tall man, and your patient is a young woman, alone in the room, who is so sick she can barely speak, it's absolutely unacceptable.  

i was able to articulate to him that i had wanted to see the results of my bloodwork before further testing.  i have been in the er many times in my life for various issues including gastric related ones, and i have never had anyone order extensive imaging before even examining me.  this clinic ordered an x-ray and ct scan, in addition to a urine sample, blood panel, and other tests,  before anyone had even examined me!! i had no unusual symptoms of any kind and in all my er experiences, the imaging comes when something shows up in bloodwork or due to symptoms noted in the exam with the doctor.  they claimed they needed imaging to see if it was appendicitis or other internal organ issue.  yet no one had even palpated my  abdomen to check for localized tenderness.  so i felt like this was a racket and i had every right to request to be seen, examined, and to know if any results in my tests indicated the need for imaging.  they had already swooped in and x-rayed my lungs and i didn't even have a cough or any symptoms remotely related.  

i was there because i needed intravenous fluids and anti-nausea meds so i could rehydrate and take tylenol, get my fever down, and be well enough to drive the next day.  i was of course willing to be examined and appreciated them looking for signs of something other than food poisoning or the flu, but this was excessive and i had every right to question them and to want to talk to the doctor about why the hell a ct scan was being ordered before anyone had talked to me. 

when my mom and i questioned them on all the testing and why we weren't being seen by a doctor, we were treated horribly.  we were gaslit, and shamed.  they then kept me there for 5.5 hours, 12-5:30am, citing being a small clinic in a rural area.  it was a monday night in the off season.  there were one or two other patients the whole time i was there and yet we went hours without being spoken to or seen. and when my mom tried to get someone's attention, to get me a blanket, or some ice chips, or any info on when we might be seen, she was told she was violating hippa laws.  by walking outside the doorway.  

anyway, this place is awful.

definitely a five star er!

the hospital is recently new.  the facility is immaculate.  the staff is personable and many are very compassionate.  the food trays are excellent and have a good variety.  guest trays are reasonably priced.  a pullout bed is available for spouses or caregivers to stay overnight.  parking is a bit of a challenge due to the number of people being served.  usually, the doctors are tops. however, i doubt that i will ever go there for care in the future.  they are clearly understaffed.  

example #1:   my wife has a bladder problem.   she had just come out of knee replacement surgery.  about 3 hours later, she wet the bed because the nurse or aide did not answer the call in a reasonable time.  other calls were made.  my wife told me that she laid in her own urine from 7:00 pm to nearly 7:00 am.  it appears that the night shift may have had too much to do.

example #2:  one of the doctors decided that she was getting too much pain medication.  without contacting the surgeon who prescribed it, the doctor adjusted (reduced) the medicine to fit his wishes.   my wife subsequently complained of severe pain.  after over an hour of intense pain (she said the pain was a 12 on a scale of 1 to 10) she was finally told that a nurse would be in in about 20 minutes.  prior to that she had also called because she was wet again.  it was about an hour and a half before she received additional pain medication and about two hours of laying in her own urine again before they came and took her to the bathroom.

example #3  while i was taking my wife's suitcase to the car, the discharge papers were being given to my wife without my presence even though i would be the caretaker for the next few weeks.    when we got home and i started reviewing the information, the names of the  drugs on the paperwork didn't even match those on the pill bottles, and the amounts were duplicated.  i literally had to write down the scripts of ten different bottles and their bottle directions so i would know what and when to give.  

example #4:  as stated above, pain did not seem to be an issue for the staff.  upon discharge, my wife was taken to my car in a wheel chair.  as soon as she was pushed to the car, the attendant left.  my wife was in so much pain and so stiff from the bandages and surgery that she was nearly unable to get into the car.  we had to have her scoot herself along the back seat with me on the other side of the back seat helping to pull her in before we could even get the doors closed...all this without anyone from the hospital staff helping.  i almost took her to back to the hospital to be readmitted as she was in so much pain that it appeared that i would not be able to  accommodate her needs.  it was about four hours later after giving her the drugs that should have been administered in  the hospital that my wife was finally relieved of much of her pain.

i started by saying that the staff is compassionate.  when someone finally did come to my wife's aid, they were very kind and willing to assist.  so was the staff guilty of  incompetence?  doubtful?  lack of staffing?  likely.
one more note.  after my wife had laid in urine for an hour and a half without assistance, i arrived in the hospital and went into the hallway to solicit help since the pager on the bed was soliciting no response.  two women (nurses or nurses aids) were sitting together talking to one another right outside of my wife's room.  one did tell me that she would get a nurse, and she also helped take my wife to the restroom and clean the bed.  but why did it take an advocate to get help?

iu claims that newsweek has given them a top ten rating for hospitals.  my experience with the care given to my wife would say the bottom ten.

came to this kaiser panorama city pharmacy for an emergency medication written by my pcp. thankfully, i looked at my member benefits and it said no charge for this medication. however, when i went to check out i was informed by the pharm tech that i need to pay retail price for it because she said it's not emergency and that routine medications are consider emergency. uhh, no sweetie, when the medication has the word "emergency" on it, it's considered emergency and medication you take every day to prevent something is not considered emergency. kaiser really need to look at education when hiring their pharmacy tech. anyways i told her to bill it to me. she said she can't do that. she finally had to ask someone else. thankfully a pharmacist who understand kaiser's policy, acknowledged that i can be billed. so when i got my bill, i was able to dispute it and got the charge removed because i quoted from the member handbook including detailed information on exclusion and inclusion and kp acknowledged it was an error. so takeaways from my experience are:

1. know your member's rights. you have the rights to the latest copy of your member handbook/member benefits. make sure you ask for it with information on all the inclusion and exclusions. it's alot of pages but read it so you can be informed of what's covered. ask for a translation in your language if you prefer (it's part of your rights).

2. if you question the cost of something and you're a kp member, ask them to bill you so you can dispute it.

3. if kaiser charges you for something that is a covered benefit, it's considered fraud. file an grievance and/or appeal with them first. if it doesn't get resolve or address within 30 days, you should notify dhcs (for medi-cal), cms (for medicare), and/or dmhc in general so an investigation can be opened. let these organizations know as well if you see quality related issues. if they get fined, they lose fundings and accreditation.

be your own advocate and know what are your rights as a patient!

i went to the emergency room for a searing 9/10 hip pain, in tears and hysterical. i wasn't really aware of my surroundings but i did have my family with me. the only thing that helped was pacing, then laying in fetal and pacing again. they put me in a room, i paced out front of it crying quietly. then a nurse at the desk told me they preferred me stay in my room. i pleaded to her hysterically that it was the only thing that helped. she rolled her eyes at me so i kept on pacing. i was in front of my room, it's not like i was freaking out walking the hospital- i don't even believe i was sobbing loudly. 
when the x-ray team arrived they were so ginger and careful and understood me. however, they found nothing. not a darn thing. so i'm here. no answers, being told i'm fine, as i experience what feels like some on twisting a pitchfork in my hip and pulling my quad muscle from my femur and knee. pleasant yes? 
at this point my husband left me with my teen son to go get our other children from school.
a woman whom ,i'm assuming was a doctor, later appeared. and at this point i was in the phase of fetal rocking. she asked me to feel around on this lump on my hip. does this hurt? no. she pushed with moderate force on my hip, triggering a dull ache, i started to cry. she proceeds to tell me i have a lipoma, a fatty tumor, that doesn't really cause pain. then she disappeared after telling me they'll get a referral started and get me discharged. that's really all i could comprehend.
i started to pace again trying to relieve the agonizing pain from the area. i think i placed myself in the floor  sobbing. now thinking back was probably the grossest thing i could have done. a lady appeared, not a doctor. she began to tell me something about orthopedic and scheduling. i told her i didn't understand what she was asking. she asked me if i could schedule a visit. i told her i didn't know. she proceeded to say dates and times and i simply could not hear her over the pain. my son handed me my phone while i lay on the floor and i opened it. i clicked on some apps, i forgot what i was looking for. i asked again what i was doing. she told me dates. i couldn't for the life of me figure out what i was supposed to do so i started to cry again. she said something and left. i now realize that she was trying to schedule me an orthopedic and follow up appointment.

this is lake norman emergency.

world-class care at a small regional hospital? who would have guessed, but it's 100% true. 

i'm an internal medicine physician (m.d; board-certified)
visiting from los angeles and was finishing dinner at a restaurant in boca with my 85 year-old dad on a saturday evening when he suddenly collapsed to the left and was having a stroke in front of my eyes. 

rushed him to boca regional medical center where they were already on high alert (we called ahead) and they implemented their "stroke alert" protocol with all hands on deck. 

on arrival, the (terrific) nurses whisked him directly from the front door to the head doc in the er (david leeman, md), he did a quick but thorough neurological assessment while dad was still in a hospital-provided wheelchair and sent him immediately to the ct scanner for a sophisticated brain perfusion scan. mind you, this all took no more than 6 minutes from er door to ct scanner (!).

ct scan showed no major blockages (thank g_d), but did show a small area that had subtly narrowed blood vessels and wasn't getting enough blood/oxygen to dad's brain for a short time. thus, the stroke symptoms at the restaurant. 

here's the best/mind-blowing part: within minutes, they had dad back from his ct scan and into one of the er's "critical care" beds, wheeled a two-way video monitor to dad's bedside and a top cleveland clinic neurologist-stroke specialist appeared live on screen and she did a remote bedside teleconsult (freshly-done ct brain perfusion scan on her computer) and chatted with/"examined" dad on the spot. 

she determined that dad had a "tia" (mini-stroke") but did not need (effective but sometimes dangerous) clot-busting drug treatment. after a team of (incredibly kind/efficient/competent) nurses took a detailed medical history, drew blood and did an ekg, they wheeled dad directly to the new marcus neuroscience inpatient unit of the hospital, where another team of great nurses attended to dad, gave him his evening meds and got him properly tucked in for the night. 

bottom line: from initial stroke symptoms to er admission to completed ct scan and expert consult/diagnosis to monitored inpatient bed, the whole process took less than 90 minutes. as stated above, world class care! 

grateful and impressed beyond words. if you need emergency care in boca, there's no better place to go

the nurses couldn't do much, since there is no doctor on the floor (no doctor on the floor) and nurses advised that internists are only available by phone and only in case of an emergency.

my mother was dry heaving, unable to swallow, short of breath at rest (all signs of late stage heart failure) and completely unattended to except by helpless nurses.  i called my brother-in-law in pittsburgh who is a well known gerontologist and read the blood results to him.  he was appalled that there hadn't been a cardiologist in to see her, nor one assigned to her. 

i asked mom's nurse dinesha to contact the two young residents who i had learned were on duty in admitting.  she called them at least 3 times over a period of 4 hours.  finally they arrived. they asked me the same questions over and over and over again. i was losing hope and patience.  i told them i wanted a cardiac consult now.

my mom was nothing more than a school project for them. one was a junior resident, dr. awadallah, the other a senior. said they would order an echo cardiogram and assured me the cardiologist would see mom in the morning. they kept telling me, "none of this is in our control." i believe them.

finally, the patient in the room next door had to be moved to icu. the icu dr came up to our floor.  he was the only doctor i'd ever encountered outside of the residents. i asked if he was a cardiologist and one of the nurses asked me, "why do you want to know?" while a compassionate nurse named ernie, quietly told me, "yes, dr. louis is a cardiologist."

my mom was dry heaving and had extreme and advancing dyspnea (breathing distress), heart palpitations, dizziness, halos around her vision, tremors, and high anxiety. all i could do was stroke her hair and watch her gasp for air.

a kind young male nurse and a super nasty female nurse reluctantly gave us oxygen, while saying, "but she doesn't need it."  as soon as the oxygen was placed, mom felt slightly better, but still shaking, dry heaving, unable to swallow, get out of bed on her own, to toilet and generally feeling very sick.

we have now called mom's cardiologist who does not have admitting privileges in this hospital.(boca regional is simply where the fire department took us.)

our cardiologist is currently searching for an available colleague with privileges at boca regional to intervene.  mom calls me just now to tell the her roomate is still screaming and she can't take any more.

i hope we can move her out of there today.

i am filing a complaint with medicare, the florida office of the inspector general, and contacting my congressman ted deutch.

i learned a big lesson and so i am sharing my experience so others aren't as naive as i was.  i was referred to the physical therapy group within presbyterian hospital dallas by my internist after having repeat back issues. i had to check in with hospital services, which should have been  a red flag since hospital charges are often much more than a private practice. i had a 1 hour evaluation where i was told i needed to work on my core muscles. i was encouraged to sign up for 1-2 sessions per week. i signed up for two per week, so i had one 1-hour evaluation and five 45 minute sessions.

i really liked the physical therapist. she was wonderful to work with. but if i had known the bill would be $3237 for these six sessions, i would have gone elsewhere. the bill was submitted to insurance, which was then  adjusted to their agreed upon price. i have to pay 100% out of pocket until i reach my deductible, so my 100% was $1578. that's $263 per session. i realize that the evaluation should cost more, but the five individual sessions included 5-10 minutes on an exercise bike -- something i could have done at home prior to arrival. this is such an insane amount for what was delivered in return and i'm no better than i was when i first walked into the place. i could have purchased at least a year's worth of exercise classes that focused on building my core instead.  

i sent an email to texas health voicing my frustration with not being told up front what my cost would be, but i haven't heard a word back, so i'm going to share my experience and hope others learn from my mistake. i'm guessing they don't care because i have to pay regardless and they're not going to do anything about it.  so... be forewarned... unless you have excellent health insurance coverage or medicare that will cover a certain number of visits, this is not the place to go for physical therapy. there are private practice physical therapists who charge much less so you can get more sessions for your money.

i am paying it down over 12 months, but it's the equivalent of having a car payment again and i really didn't need this expense right now. in addition to still having back issues i came here to address, i now have a huge amount of stress trying to figure out how i can come up with these monthly payments. lesson learned.

i'm giving 2 stars only because i liked my physical therapist.

having had previous, unavoidable experiences with robert wood's emergency room, it was with a mixture of trepidation and dread that i found myself once more walking through the emergency room entrance. previously, my father had often been a patient there due to a long battle with cancer which necessitated several trips to this particular emergency room.  at that time i had never before experienced such a complete disregard for basic patient care in an emergency room setting.
so when my elderly mother was transported there after a very serious fall this past week i was shocked as to how little has changed. this was a monday afternoon however you would have thought it was new year's eve - the waiting room was a war zone. at least forty people were cramped inside - patients were sitting on the floor - vomit was on the floors, in the bathrooms and even in front of the entrance! several heavily armed policeman stood looking menacingly at every person checking in. my mother was already in the er so i was waiting in line to check in. not knowing what her status was i was understandably anxious to get back to see her. however, i had to wait in line with patients that were checking in. as hipaa does not appear to be something that this hospital is familiar with, i was privy to most of these patients entire medical history. this was unavoidable as the receptionist loudly repeated it back to the patient, in front of all of us standing there. i became even more outraged when it became evident that most of the patients there were using the emergency room for their primary care - issues included stomach aches, slight fevers, colds, headaches, etc. - which were non emergencies and could have been dealt with at a pcp appointment. 
upon finally getting my "clearance" to go back to the emergency room (i had to have my id scanned - was told that weapons and/or drugs are not allowed - i felt like saying that the brooks brothers topcoat i was wearing does not have inner pockets large enough to hold a glock and meth just to be snarky however with two police officers glaring at me i felt it more prudent to just hold my tongue and press on).
once back in the emergency room i was disappointed to see that although the interior had been updated their view on quality of care remained the same. when my father was there he and several other patients were lined up on guerneys in the hallway for hours - one visit my father was in the hallway for 7 hours!
i arrived to find the same scene - row after row of patients lined up on stretchers against the walls. i found my elderly mother next to the nurses station covered in blood from severe facial lacerations. and then the wait began ..... one hour no nurse/no doctor; two hours the same; three hours the same. i was given a wash basin so i could wash the blood off my mom's face and hands. 
as this hospital once again has no conception of hipaa i found out from the team of doctors and nurses hovering over the patient in front of us that he came in with what he thought was chest pains - however he said it could have been indigestion from the two double cheeseburgers he ate. the young woman behind use was going through chemotherapy and was severally ill - once again staff went through her medical history for all to hear. 
i am generally a very patient person. i cannot begin to understand the stress that the staff in these settings are put under. however after 4 hours without a nurse or doctor even having the courtesy to stop and just apologize for the delay my patience was at an end. i stopped the nearest nurse and demanded that my mother be seen.
well amazingly enough a neurology intern and two nurses appeared out of thin air. they said it was busy but they would follow up and try to get my mother out of the hallway and into one of the er bays.
after 2 more hours she was finally moved to a semi private bay.
my niece who is a nurse practitioner arrived and thankfully took charge. the remainder of my mom's stay went relatively smoothly due to my niece's non stop advocacy.

the complex is large and if you have multiple appointments in different buildings as i did. just ask the nurse assisting you to request a shuttle and they will get you to were you need to go. instead of moving your car over and over and dealing with the parking.

depending on what you're in for will dictate what floor/building you will be placed in. post op recovery icu is 2nd floor of main building and god bless if that's what you're in for.

nursing staff along with the np(nurse practitioner, don't call them a dr even if they're right there) have some of the most gentle care i've experienced from any hospital. i've bee. to other sharps and i can wholeheartedly say this hospital takes the prize. from providing you with as much information as possible to assist you in your recovery to ensuring you help is merely a call away by providing you with their direct number(they're given a cell phone at work so they can be reached by you or the nurses station if needed urgently) these ladies and gentleman embody care. my hats off to floor 6 (cardiac recover) for all the outstanding service and care they provided me. i honestly don't think i would have been recovering as well as i am without their support and care.

food is still none the less hospital food but i was able to speak with the chef in charge and here their plans for the coming year. adopting a comprehensive plan to ensure that the food quality and nutritional value are in keeping with the care provided at the hospital. a one of a kind program that already has made staples in improving the quality of the food and nutritional value(small steps so far such as switching from iceberg lettuce to green leaf lettuce and such). my hats off to them for improving this overlooked aspect in hospitals. the ordering system is fantastic how they take your meal order ahead of time to not interfere with your recovery and to ensure that you designated meal with restrictions if any get to you on time. i lived how each .real came with a nutritional overview letting you k ow nutrients, calories, etc in your meal. loved that!

radiology/radiologist as i had to deal with frequently were friendly and helpful. whether they had to assist me in my room or take me down to get mris(be aware, its always the coldest part of the building because they do have to keep those machines cool or they can burnout so ask for bra blanket if you need it). the transport team who assisted you getting from location to location or helping you leave in the end were always kind, helpful and made sure you knew you were always welcomed back.... hopefully not soon though.

all in all if i could rate this hospital a 11 or higher i would! excellent is the only word i can come up with to describe the care provided by the staff at sharp memorial. my hats off to all the staff that help in the recovery of the many patients who walk through their doors and the supporting staff behind the scenes.

doc_text:
a couple of years ago the nyu langone er, cobble hill (also fabulous) sent me to nyu langone, brooklyn by ambulance for pneumonia.  i was hospitalized for seven days.  when i was dismissed i felt like i was leaving a large community of old friends. 

the cobble hill er gave me a choice of nyu langone brooklyn or manhattan, where my grandson was born.  i knew nothing about the brooklyn hospital except the fact that it would be an easier subway trip from my son's office in lower manhattan & closer to their home in brooklyn. and i certainly wanted visitors.

the hospital, formerly lutheran, is a large older hospital with shared rooms.  but that wasn't a problem.  in fact it made me happy to nurture my last roommate through some of her health care fears.

the staff was awesome!! i can't say enough good things about the entirety, from the doctors all the way to the attendants who took me to radiology.

nyu langone is a teaching hospital.  so i had 3 specialty teams treating me and trying to discover the root cause of my months long bout with pneumonia.  from the specialists, to their residents, to their interns to their med students, i received excellent care.  the specialty teams coordinated, getting together to discuss my case.

they performed an enormous amount of testing in addition to treatments.  when the specialty teams would visit, they would discuss their findings and answer all my questions.  i really felt i was in excellent hands.

but the good and friendly care also came from the nurses, nursing technicians, food service workers, lab technicians, breathing specialists, swallow specialists, orderlies and housekeeping staff.  have i forgotten anyone. many would hang out in my room.  it doesn't have to be miserable being in the hospital, even if you're really sick.  it can be fun.

it was fun pretending my hospital bed was traveling the bqe as we rushed down the halls to radiology.  (i have to admit it was my idea.) it was fun when the pulmonary specialist took a picture of my iphone because i had over 60,000 unread emails.  it was fun making someone smile who seemed to not have smiled in a long time.  

the meals were very good for hospital fare, although i didn't enjoy having to be on a heart healthy diet.  each morning food services would come around for the daily menu choices.  they were very good about bringing extra coffee and goodies.  i didn't starve as i've felt in other hospitals.

and they were attentive.  i've been in a hampton roads hospital in terrible pain in the middle of the night while the nursing staff ignored my continual buzzing for help.  not so at nyu langone, brooklyn.

even though i was close to the nursing desk i could sleep.  as much as they will let you sleep in a hospital..... :)

when i was dismissed many staff came to give me a goodbye hug.  it felt like leaving a group of friends.

the hospital scheduled the follow up appointments with nyu doctors.  they checked on me afterwards.  i was also given a followup nurse number that i could call.

the nyu langone app is fabulous.  i can still see all the results of my testing, both at the hospital and the cobble hill er.  the catscan reports are extremely detailed.  i wish the hampton roads hospitals provided radiology readings with such detail.

i would not hesitate to go back to nyu langone, brooklyn.  my care was wonderful.

emergency medical treatment & labor act (emtala)

in 1986, congress enacted the emergency medical treatment & labor act (emtala) to ensure public access to emergency services regardless of ability to pay. section 1867 of the social security act imposes specific obligations on medicare-participating hospitals that offer emergency services to provide a medical screening examination (mse) when a request is made for examination or treatment for an emergency medical condition (emc), including active labor, regardless of an individual's ability to pay. hospitals are then required to provide stabilizing treatment for patients with emcs. if a hospital is unable to stabilize a patient within its capability, or if the patient requests, an appropriate transfer should be implemented.

i went to holy cross for a knee replacement.  the doctor was great and replacement doing good. however, when i came home i was on pain meds with tylenol.  doctors told me i most likely acquired a gram negative ecoli infection from the urinary catheter. the infection then grew into my blood and i became sepsis. after a week in another hospital and sent home with a mid line iv for antibiotics. i recovered after three weeks. i called holy cross hospital infectious department to let them know.  well i received no concern, no caring, and an excuse that i only had the catheter for one day. they also said, in order to pick up this infection in the hospital i would have had to have the catheter two days.  so not a very educated answer.  infections are acquired through direct contact and time exposure plays no role. 

copied from the internet:

causes
bacteria are normally found throughout the body including on the skin and in the intestines. when kept in balance, bacteria can help the body work normally. however, an imbalance of the bacteria or passing of bacteria to areas where there are no bacteria, can lead to an infection. an infection will develop if large amounts of bacteria are present, the bacteria are aggressive, or the immune system is weakened.

common ways for bacteria to pass to vulnerable parts of the body include:

use of medical devices that pass into the body, such as iv or urinary catheters
open wounds
contact with someone who has or has been exposed to gram-negative bacteria
risk factors
hospitalization is the most common risk factor for gram-negative bacterial infections. the longer the stay in the hospital, the higher the risk of infection.

other factors that increase the risk of a bacterial infection include:

recent surgery
use of urinary catheter
war wounds
dialysis for kidney disease , which includes regular use of iv lines or catheters
mechanical ventilator use
weakened immune system

with my experience it doesn't matter how good the doctor is.  if the hospital is a sick hospital, even the most mild surgery could cause sickness or even death. do your research.

mclaren's billing:

my husband had a stroke december 2019. he was rushed to mclaren northern michigan hospital in petoskey. frankly, i felt my head was in a fog most of the time and i was just so glad he came out of it alive. he had rehab done locally in january and had to have a follow-up with the neurologist february 3rd. doctor said that they cannot find a reason for my husband having a stroke and he needed to have a loop recorder placed inside his chest to see if he has a-fib.  february 7th he has that put in.  today (february 26) i am sitting at my desk paying $1,300 in co-pays for the things he had done - i admit it is a bit steep for us but praising god my husband is still alive. however, as i was paying by phone with mclaren, they let me know that there was a bill for $11,000.00 coming down the pike that wasn't covered by bcbs. it was the loop recorder. they called and asked for a pre-authorization for the loop to be placed in and was told by bcbs that they didn't one - no mention that it wasn't a covered benefit; the doctor's office didn't ask and bcbs didn't offer them the information. how does two retired people on social security suppose to pay for their mistake because each one blames the other for not getting the information and we are stuck with the bill? 

paying on these bills are equally as hard because all you get from mclaren's is the dollar amount - you really have no idea what you are paying on (it isn't itemized). also, when paying online through your bank, you have to input each bill into your system as each bill has its own unique account number. so you may have a dozen bills (like we have) and each one has its own account number - very time-consuming having to pay online.

my google review of albemarle hospital was shadowbanned, ie., censored, so here i go on yelp to alert the public. these events are old, but they give insight to albemarle hospital's problems which go back to old style politics within the physicians themselves and the hospital board.
in 6 years before i arrived, albemarle had cycled through 5 orthopedic surgeons and while i was there at least 6 more came and left.  i was suspended three times as a physician at albemarle hosp. first for chewing out a  registration worker who had refused to register a patient in the waiting room who was in tears. this  registration worker was female, black and addressed her grievance with the title of "minister." with god on her side, she could do no wrong. the 2nd suspension was because i did not come in to see an "emergency" patient, even though i had gone on courtesy staff a few months earlier! when i returned 4 days later from my trip, this patient was sitting in the wheelchair in the parking lot smoking. some emergency. nothing had been done for his dislocated total hip by my competitor dr watson, except to report me! my third suspension was a summary suspension for my complaining to kathy fairfax, surgical head rn, about how the administrator sharon tanner was running the hospital financially into the ground. (reportedly $40 million in the green when she started, $100 million in the red when she was escorted out under police guard.) i was labeled a "disruptive physician" despite three negative evaluations by a harassing nc medical board. nevertheless, i was exiled for 3 months to hattiesburg ms pine grove "treatment center" for "anger management" where i was suddenly diagnosed and treated as a drug addict/alcoholic! there had never been any issue of either drugs or alcohol in my entire life! no "anger management" was offered. quite hypocritically, edward eadie, md chief of surgery, and ralph battles md, chief of staff,  who were both signing my suspensions, had histories of having physically assaulted nurses! when i returned from my 3 months exile, it was learned that my "replacement," dr kona, was the alcoholic.  kathy fairfax then left shortly thereafter for florida.  then i discovered neurosurgeon  dr sonnino had refused to come in to see a post-op spine case with an epidural abscess. his patient ultimately died after being shipped to virginia. this was all  kept quiet and he was suddenly "rescued" with creation of the position of "chief medical officer and vice president of quality" with a  $275,000 salary by tanner now that he was no longer insurable for such an egregious patient abandonment. but my hip patient was supposed "to have set the precedent for future acts like this" according to eadie. i guess not! these are the games that go on in hospitals. nothing has changed.   eadie, battles may you burn in hell for what you did to me!  meanwhile, the nc medical board is not protecting the public either. it is public relations management and they served me up as a poster child to  launch their new crusade against the so called "disruptive physician."  and you wonder why i was so angry?
don't take my word for it. check out my story. you wouldn't believe it.  karl w hubbard md

the following is based on recent visit to the er.

background: busy flu season.  hospital had been on diversion recently.  ip beds full.  er very crowded.  placed in area outside main er.

first, the positives.  these er staff were excellent:

firenze b - very understanding
ben, rn

management/professionalism:

felt like there was very little physician or rn oversight or presence in the er. no sense of leadership presence. this erodes patient/family confidence in staff ability to provide appropriate care, competently and timely.  this is heightened by fact that a lot of staff only a few years out of school.  

staff were observed discussing personal issues, staff-staff issues/gossip, other patients, vacation plans, "crazy people", etc.  discussing patients in areas where others (everyone) could hear.

staff need coaching: e.g., christopher d., rn - did not treat patients with respect and dignity (despite patients being challenging); i observed his demeanor with one challenging patient in particular; it is never ok for any staff member to be rude, argumentative, dismissive, and poke fun at a patient - or anyone for that matter; terrible. this rn threatened to withhold meds "next time i won't give it to you." laughing, rn said, "it's almost entertaining...you have to laugh at it" referring to the patient.  another rn had to take over caring for the patient.

lack of attention to patients - hours would go by w/out staff attending to a patient.  what is rounding protocol?

noisy - staff loud and boisterous in late evening and early morning hours - disruptive and not at all conducive to healing 

upon arrival to er check in - rn kelly wore mask but later had it pulled down below chin.  rn in nearby room celebrated he had just seen his "last patient" before his shift ends, but noted unfortunately he had to fill out some sort of paperwork; he held up a folder with a pink sheet of paper

masks - lackadaisical approach by many staff with respect to wearing flu mask - either pulled fully off face or wore half on - below nose.

musical chairs - patients left in chairs (not enough beds); moved several times within the same ancillary/accessory side area: why?

cramped spaces - er berths only as wide as a bed, with flimsy partitions that would not always stay in position.  very little (no) privacy.

providers (resident? and student) - using patient spouse for medical (clinical) translation to get medical history, document symptoms.  staff knew little or no spanish.

while the hospital was extremely busy (flu season), there is never any excuse for staff to act in the ways described.  this behavior is unsafe, provides a poor patient experience, and undercuts the work of team overall.  i encountered many (named above) excellent, caring team members.

i hope this feedback improves care and environment at nyu winthrop.  i want this hospital to thrive in our community.  we have much need for healthcare access.

i had two outpatient eye surgeries in 2014 and everything was fine.  i recently had a two-day in-patient knee replacement and i was seriously disappointed.   everything was fine with the surgery as before but the in-patient stay was horrific.   it was like staying in a stripped-down cheap motel 6.  the staffing was limited.  they encouraged you to have someone spend the night with you post surgery.  there were strangers roaming the hallways and patients were in single rooms.  it was scary.  the only persons i saw the first night were male attendants who helped me to the bathroom.  there is no in-house food service.  it is all brought in on trays like airplane service.  meals were microwaved and you are given flimsy plastic silverware that broke when you used it.  the day following surgery, no one came to check on me until 10 a.m.  the nurse?came in and i asked when breakfast was coming and she informed me that breakfast was over and there was no food.  eventually, a man came in in a white coat and pulled two small cereal boxes from his pocket and announced "breakfast is here!"  no bowl, milk or silverware.  they don't keep any juice, crackers, yogurt or jello for post-surgical patients who might come out of anesthesia with a queasy stomach.   there were no
amenities nor creature comforts like a carafe of ice water in your room, a towel or facecloth to wash up.   there was a bed, tray table and chair in the room and lousy tv service.  it was a cold, spare, soul less place.

the physical therapists were two older teens who helped me walk across the hall once and then showed me how to push a walmart bag back and forth while i sat in a chair.  i was never given a discharge meeting and was told ten minutes before i was picked up that an ambulance was coming to transfer me.  it was friday and they do not want to staff over the weekends so everyone was supposed to leave by noon.  i believe the kids might have been summer employees as it was summertime.

this is a doctor-owned facility and it is truly bare bones and they are pinching every last penny there.  the only good thing was the nurse who started my iv got it on the first try and it was painless.  kudos to her!  i would never go there again as an inpatient.  it was too barebones for me and scary at night if you were alone.  i think the out-patient surgery staff is good but the inpatient staff needs a lot of training and employees.

parking at 2 am in a snowstorm on monday night was simple enough and the waiting room was empty...score! first problem, i was parched and the soda machine in the waiting room stole my money. 

the triage clerk would win no awards, but with nobody else around, it was unremarkable positive or negative. 

once inside the er, the nurses were fantastic and remained so throughout. then the problems. i was treated by a physician's assistant who had the personality of a phone book and the skill of a kid still developing motor control playing operation.  i received a local anesthetic and the pa told me the finger must be good and numb. i insisted, no, there is zero loss of sensitivity in the finger for the simple reason because there was zero loss of sensitivity in the finger. somehow i was convinced to allow the pa to start draining the infection. each poke by his scalpel or needle-mind you well after the anesthesia should have kicked in-resulted in searing bolts of pain. the genius pa shouted "sir.  you're in an er, you must be quiet!"  i replied "there is only a single patient here besides me, a super fat pregnant woman demanding benzos. you need to remove your incompetent hands from me and gtf away from me. i'm leaving." 

then, unbelievably, it got comically worse as i did consent to the pa's attending physician to have a look. like the amazing way donald trump has actually made george w. bush seem competent in comparison, the attending arrived ungroomed, in a stained shirt and with distinct bo, and managed to improve my perception of the pa (only in comparison). 

i dismissed the attending. the fantastic nurses bandaged up my finger and i proceeded to get dressed for winter weather, which took some time since i was one handed then. knowing the nurses couldn't say anything, but equally well knowing they had to know the incompetence of those two losers who "treated" me, i trash talked the pa and the odoriferous attending during this lengthy process to give them a voice they were surely denied in public. 

in closing, i note that nancy w writes in response to these reviews the same insincere boilerplate so often that i am sure she has a macro since it is called upon all too often. i hope that nancy u or whomever reviews these matters does not cherrypick my kind words for the nurses as praise, because my encounter with mather was a breathtaking failure. all of the negative reviews posted here look credible to me. the positive reviews are written by people too unsophisticated to know they had shitty care (a good outcome does not necessarily  mean you received good care) or who happened to be lucky or not seriously sick or injured

i do not recommend this clinic.  i saw drs. pemberton and gopal, and would not recommend either.  

i first went  to this clinic because of excruciating menstrual pain.  after waiting quite a while, i was seen by a woman who only later identified herself as a student and not an actual gynecologist.  i had made an appointment to see a doctor, not a student.  i understand that students need to learn, but i should've been notified of this when i made the appointment, and asked if this was an acceptable substitution (it was not).  what should've been a 20 minute appointment became 1 1/2 hours because the student kept having to excuse herself to go talk to the actual doctors, recount to them what i'd just said, get their feedback, and then come tell me what they'd said.  it was like a terrible game of telephone, and not at all professional.  please note that they billed my insurance as though i'd seen an actual doctor.

i had to come back for a biopsy.  dr. pemberton offered no pain control options for the procedure and just told me to "relax".  ultimately, it was unsuccessful because she said my cervix was "being shy", so i had to make another appointment, take a cervical relaxer, and come back.  i did this, and the biopsy happened...but it was the most painful thing i've ever experienced (and i've passed kidney stones!!)!  at one point, i screamed for her to stop, and she did not.  that's not okay, and i felt violated, but also felt like i had no other options, given the physical position i was in.  

i was diagnosed, medicated, and while this helped, it didn't completely fix the issue.  i then had to go back and negotiate treatment options with dr. gopal, because dr. pemberton was on temporary leave.  he refused to even consider a hysterectomy, because he said "i might want to carry a child someday"...even though i explained to him that that wasn't going to happen for a number of reasons.  what is this, the 1950's, where keeping my lady-parts so i can reproduce is more important than treating the very real medical issue i have???  dr. gopal offered other options that included a lot of disruptive medications and unnecessary medical procedures, none of which will actually address the issue directly, and instead made it clear that he doesn't really have any real solutions, but doesn't want to admit that he doesn't know what else to do.

i'm not including all the medical details, because frankly it's private, but let's just say i'm beyond frustrated.  i am medically-savvy enough about my own body and the medical issues i have to know that i'm getting sub-par care.  i understand that medical science has limitations, especially for women's bodies, and especially when it comes to gynecological issues.  but i'm also not going to let myself be experimented on like a guinea pig by someone who clearly isn't taking me seriously and who wants to subject me to unnecessary medical interference that isn't actually a solution, more like an expensive, exhausting, painful, time-consuming distraction.

this practice clearly focuses on pregnancy and childbirth, rather than complex gynecological problems that have nothing to do with actual reproduction, something i wasn't aware of when i was referred to it by a different, well-meaning doctor.

this office isn't fully wheelchair-accessible (turn radii are too tight, furniture is placed poorly, doors are hard to operate, none of the staff has ever offered to assist me).    

i would not recommend the cpmc women's center based on my experience.  i am currently looking for a different gynecologist.
