dentists and oral surgeons and orthopedic surgeons, a recuperative care center, a church and even a crisis house. and right now, i am at grossmont hospital in la mesa, california, where on march 2nd, 2020 i underwent total knee replacement surgery. now don't get me wrong, i trust and appreciate my surgeon, dr. michael sirota. i trusted him enough to let him cut me open and put in a fake knee while i was unconscious and helpless. i trust and respect his staff, especially rose martin, who went above and beyond to make sure i kept my surgery date. but from the moment of my joint replacement class through intake and waking up in recovery, i have received the best care i've ever gotten, physical, mental and spiritual. and i mean by everybody i've come into contact with, phlebotomists, nursing assistants, the social worker, intake folks, my surgeon's assistant, the meal hostess, the nursing students, the chaplain, the physical therapists... every single one has been as though they were snapped up out of the best, funniest, most soulful, helpful and charming medical comedy/drama film ever made. now, i have to be brutally honest, i have been on some strong pain medicine, but nothing that has significantly altered my cognitive ability. unfortunately, it has caused me to forget some of the names of a few of the remarkably compassionate, funny, kind, competent medical professionals i have ever had the privilege to be cared for by. but it has truly been the nurses and nursing assistants who have saved me here. over the last nearly 4 years, i have lost the love of my life, two close friends, a cousin i grew up with and my dear little dog. i came here angry and tearful and hopeless. i actually expected to wake up from surgery missing a leg. so, here goes. the nurses...lizzy, young, funny, immensely caring. she stayed over after shift change when she'd been up for the whole night shift taking care of me, because i was scared and in pain. she stayed past her work day (night) until she was sure i was ok. mikell who was so compassionate and thoughtful that he made my bed into a cozy cocoon so i could sleep comfortably even though my leg was excruciatingly painful. loretta, who liked to pretend she was just a no nonsense health care worker, but helped me bathe and go to the bathroom and learn to safely get in and out of bed when i could barely move without pain and never once made me feel embarrassed or desperately dependent. martha, whose quiet, peaceful competence made me feel safe and as cared for as when i was a child...and my childhood through my adolescence and adulthood was plagued by illness and injury. and dina, a straight forward, no nonsense nurse who ended up not only caring for my physical well-being, but gave me the straight forward other caregivers had been while i was crying with sheer gratitude over the  incredible staff at grossmont hospital in la mesa, california. if i have missed someone, i am sincerely sorry, it is only honorhealth south tempe is in my neighborhood, just a half-mile away, so getting there couldn't be more convenient.

the two nurse practitioners, though, were much more invested in doing what primary-care providers ought to do, especially stephanie piercy, who is now my official primary-care provider.

an absolute horror show, travesty of medical care, and a lawsuit waiting to happen. 

my mom fell this week (fragile, dementia, history of stroke, and a hip replacement). i called 911 and on scene the paramedics asked which hospital we preferred- i chose mercy general as her pcp and records are all at dignity health. 

worst decision ever. 
how the hospital is run: 
a doctor saw my mom for a total of 1 minute at arrival and 30 seconds at exit. no supervision or accountability. lots of people here seemed "checked out" working in an untenable environment. 

medical assistants and one rn is on duty, one pa or doctor for what seemed to be 50 or more patients. there are lots of guys in green outfits doing, apparently, nothing that i noticed for the five hours we were there. my mom was parked on a gurney for the whole time in a busy hallway. people, patients, staff, gurneys, paramedics, security guards, and random people coming and going nonstop. 

she had imaging of her hip, elbow, and arm. there were good people doing the imaging. i repeated that her head hurt- mom chimed in- and then that was related to the doctor and a ct was ordered. too bad the doctor refused to talk to the patient and just felt  her bones for minute and didn't ask one question to her "patient" aka just a number.  props to the imaging team for maintaining a system and compassion for patients in a totally chaotic situation. 

she was offered a tylenol and glass of water. no updates on what was happening...i assumed a room would be provided eventually.  other patients parked in hallway, including a man and his wife- he begged to have someone help her use the restroom- for an hour. 

at about 8:30 pm the medical assistant popped by and said no broken bones, mom had to get up and prove she could walk before being released. i stepped in when mom got upright on the gurney and said she felt dizzy. 

medical assistant said she would have a chair behind mom as she walks. my dad was helping. honest to god, this was the plan. my mom fell, said she's dizzy, and they want her to walk in a busy hallway with people crashing around pell-mell. 

i spoke up loudly, said you need to get an orderly and she said, this is how we do it do you have a better suggestion? 

this could have been solved by having my mom move to a room- (literally across the hall an empty room with three hospital beds) for a safe environment for a trial run. 

we worked with situation at hand with me guarding the hall like a pit bull behind mom and blocking people and gurneys from coming through....and dad ready to catch mom. and then medical assistant tells mom to get back to 
the gurney after a successful trial run. mom has lymphedema and her swollen legs would be hitting metal. i said no get a wheelchair. then a guy in green shows up. apparently ready to catch mom if she falls. thanks, perfect timing. 

so, end of story- doctor comes by for 30 seconds to tell us no broken bones and runs off, totally masked  to protect herself from coronavirus. brava. medical assistant turned out to be a nice person and she stood by us while my dad got car. she was smart and empathetic once she was freed from caring for 50 people simultaneously with no tangible support. 

literally the worst er i have ever been in. train wreck, third world care. danger. no info. a few decent people trying to do their best in a disaster scene. never again. they should close their doors if they can't serve patients and provide a baseline of medical care. our east sac family has been born cared for. and died at mercy for three generations. sadly, switching care to sutter asap. 

every person who walks out of these doors should get a t-shirt that says, "i survived mercy er."

suggestion: hire some nuns to get this place shipshape. someone needs to be slapping a ruler.

it makes all the difference if you have a good nurse. 

joanne - er nurse today 1/1 /2020 5 stars

my husband has been to er's 3 times in the last 6 weeks. 1 surgery, 3 ultrasounds, 1 mri, 1 endoscopy, 1 ct scan, two hospital stays 3 days or more. believe me when i tell you, we know a good nurse from a nurse who's phoning it in. joanne is a great nurse.

what makes for a good nurse? actually caring for a patient as a person. being gentle when putting in an iv. thinking about what will make the patient comfortable and alleviate anxiety. cleanliness. good communication. asking good questions and listening to the answer. following through as promised. 

it doesn't matter how many years you've been a nurse because we've had some who are very seasoned and some in training. it comes from something within, a genuine empathy and kindness. i don't think you can teach it, you either have it or you don't. joanne has it. 

also a very special shout out to our er doctor today, dr elizabeth owen. she is one of those rare gems who tries to figure out what is actually wrong with you. not just mask the pain with painkillers. she is genuinely trying to solve the mystery of my husband's pain and help him heal. she spent more time with us today taking about possible causes and remedies than the surgeon who had done the procedure and any of the rounds doctors on our hospital stays. i truly appreciate a doctor who is hell bent on figuring out a puzzle.

hard to overstate the level of bullshit you have to put up with at kaiser. without extreme self advocacy you will get nowhere. there was no better metaphor for my experience here than when one of the nurses checking people in was counting money in the cash register for five minutes instead of checking in people in the line for urgent care. 

situation a
i injure my achilles in winter 2017 and via my employer, i change insurance to kaiser to start 2018. i set an appointment for my achilles and am told i will have to see a general doctor who can write a recommendation to see another doc for an ultrasound/mri/etc. doc 1 sends me to doc 2. doc 2 misdiagnoses the achilles injury via ultrasound and recommends physical therapy. two doctor visits and one month have passed and i have received no treatment, now on my way to doc 3. i do physical therapy for three months (would later find out this was all done on a partially torn achilles) not surprisingly, ankle makes no progress. probably tore it worse in pt. five months down, i've made no progress and finally doc 4 prescribes an mri. now i have a correctly diagnosed interstitial tear and can begin actually recovering in a walking boot. over one year after the initial injury and i am nowhere near returning to running.

situation b
i have an ear infection. doc at urgent care correctly prescribes flouroquinolone drops, but does not insert a wick to get the antibiotic past the swelling down to the ear drum. two days later the ear drum is more painful and nearly completely swollen shut. i come back into urgent care and the check in nurse tries to shove a thermometer in the ear i just told her was infected. finally sit down with the doc, and without warning he shoves the wick straw into my swollen shut ear--worst pain i've felt since getting stung by a stingray. 

situation c
i get back from travelling abroad and go to urgent care for bad flu symptoms. doc gives me a flu swab (much more painful than it sounds). i sit in the waiting room for one hour waiting for the results. tired of waiting and feeling like hell i go knock on the door, nurse says the lab has not sent results back. they contact the lab, lab has forgotten to send results. 20 minutes later doc says results are negative and recommends sleep and fluids. meanwhile, my friend on the trip has the same symptoms, and random local doctor in the san juan islands correctly diagnoses travelers diarrhea and azithromycin. friend is fine in 24 hours. two days of feeling like hell later, i return to urgent care to request azithromycin.

to all those insured with kaiser, good luck and godspeed.

brought my 5 year old son here last week not because he was experiencing cold symptoms but because he had also started wheezing when breathing and also vomiting. he had no fever but the wheezing concerned me because he has never had any issues with breathing or any asthma related issues. 
all the staff that helped were wonderful and friendly. 
they gave him some breathing treatments which really helped with the wheezing. they also did chest x-rays and tested for flu and strep. tests came back negative and x-rays looked fine. doctor said his lungs were reacting to something, possible allergy or asthma related, so he prescribed an asthma pump and a couple medications for nausea and his chest. 
came in at 3am, left around 7:30am. 

now almost a week later, my son woke up at 3:30am with a 104 fever that wouldn't go down. brought him in at 7:30am, was brought in immediately which was surprising to me because usually they make us wait a bit. doctor originally was going to just test again for flu because my boyfriend recently tested positive for it, and give him a bunch of fluids because his heart rate was out the roof. they also did some blood work. while we were waiting for results, he started screaming, crying, and clutching his stomach. this went on for 30 minutes before they were able to give him motrin which helped with the pain and fever. at this point i believe his temp was 102, heart rate still above 150. he also started vomiting a lot. now this concerned the doctor more also because his blood work showed his white blood cell count was 24 and normally should be 8-10. she said that was showing that his body is trying to fight something off so something was wrong. because he was clutching the  right side of his stomach, they thought it was possibly his appendix so he went off for an ultrasound. they couldn't see his appendix because his bladder was full and he did not want to pee so the result was that the doctor thought he might've had appendicitis and we were transferred to hartford hospital because it's a dedicated children's hospital and if it was appendicitis, he would have to have surgery to remove his appendix. waterbury hospital does not have a pediatric department. 
we were transferred about noon and got to hartford hospital about 12:30. 
once there we were seen immediately by a bunch of staff. he got an ultrasound done and appendix looked normal. they did more x-rays on him and turns out he had pneumonia (they could see it in the x-rays and doctor says it explains his fever, and abdominal pain). they diagnosed him in about an hour and a half, and we were out by 3. 
so....he had pneumonia since the first er trip we took but instead he was diagnosed with asthma and this second trip was diagnosed with possible appendicitis scaring me to death! why couldn't they see the pneumonia when they did the x-rays the first time from the very beginning?! extremely frustrating!!

still, the staff that helped me during this time were all great, friendly, and treated my son very well. 
i took 1 star off because of the wait time that always seems to be a problem and another star because of the improper diagnoses, not once but twice. 
i should've known though because when i came here for myself awhile back, they tested me for strep and although it came back negative, i was still prescribed strep medication for whatever reason. unbelievable! 
anyways, if you're coming here for your children, know they do not have a pediatric department so either go to saint mary's or i highly recommend hartford's children emergency department, worth the longer drive trust me!!!!

i was an rn for many years (cardiology icu) and took excellent care or many, many people. now when i need to be cared for i'm not getting it.

i can only assume that cu anschutz has a centralized great paper shredder where they send all referrals, medical records, and requests to insurance companies.

my husband had a fantastic doctor in the neurology department who helped him finally get the treatment he needed... after months of struggling through lost paperwork, unreturned calls, etc.  then the doctor submitted a request to the insurance company, but that must have gone to the great paper shredder too, because the insurance company never received it.  required several more phone calls and waiting, resulting in a couple months delay in treatment.  the whole time, the doctor never got any of the messages he was leaving for him.  not great when you have a neurodegenerative disease.

then we moved out of state, and after two months of weekly phone calls to try to get his records sent to the new hospital with no luck, the new hospital finally gave up and went in and pulled his records electronically.

two years later, we are moving back, and i try to make an appointment with the pelvic pain clinic.  different department... maybe it was just neurology that couldn't handle paperwork.  nope.  sent a referral, and just got a "we don't have anything."  still can't make an appointment.  i'm in a lot of pain, have been for years, nobody's figured it out yet, and just as i'm moving/switching doctors, i'm having a really bad reaction to the latest birth control they've tried to put me on as treatment.  i'd like to at least have an appointment lined up, because i know it can sometimes take months to see a specialist.  meanwhile the meds are making the pain worse as well as causing my head to feel like it's floating off into space like a balloon.

i asked, is there a number that my doctor could call to make sure that my referral is received this time?  answer:  "no, it goes somewhere else."  yeah, it must go to the great paper shredder to join all of my husband's medical records, phone messages, and insurance requests.

their suggestion is for me to hand-deliver the referral, thus circumventing the great paper shredder that relentlessly guards the fax machine exit.  sure, let me just get in my car and drive 18 hours to hand-deliver a fax.

their next best suggestion is to have my doctor's office staff write "second attempt" at the top of the referral.  perhaps the great paper shredder does not have a taste for the words "second attempt."  i'm not optimistic.

too bad, because the doctors and researchers there seem quite good, and it seems to be the best or only place in the state to go for some health issues.

well, i don't like leaving negative reviews but this experience was really just inappropriate. i went in to the er with kind of a slew of symptoms as i've been sick for about 6 months. i try not to be difficult as i understand that being a triage doctor is no easy task. but the doc that i saw in triage kept laughing at me whenever i answered his questions. i came in with severe chest pain and was having trouble taking a deep breathe and was quite scared. he made fun of me because i told him i didn't want a chest x-ray and then pushed it on me. after that, he insisted that i was probably pregnant. now i know that a pregnancy test in the er is pretty standard, but he really kept insinuating that my chest pain could be related to pregnancy. and made fun of me when i told him that i wasn't. he could have just said that it was a test they do before an x-ray or literally anything other than respond by laughing and condescending to me. the test was negative. 
once i got to a bed my new doc was so nice and really explained everything well. told me i needed an mri of my neck, as i hadn't been able to eat for two days and that i could do that outside of the er. i was really relieved that i was okay and could leave. but when the woman came with my discharge papers, she got upset that i had a passport instead of drivers license and then said that i didn't meet my deductible so i needed to pay up front. i asked if my insurance could bill me and she laughed and said, "obviously, and it's going to be a lot because you didn't meet your deductible." my boyfriend was in the room and asked out of curiosity what the deductible was and the woman yelled, "she's not even sick!" and just left. 
if it had just been the first doc that kept laughing at me i wouldn't have written this. but there's just really no need to treat people this way. i understand how hard and taxing those jobs are. my whole family works in the medical field and my sis is a nurse. but i was quiet, respectful, and never complained. but no matter what i did i got quite awful treatment that honestly had me leave in tears.
working at an er is stressful. but people are at their most vulnerable when they come into one and should be treated with at least some decency.

doc_text:
maternity out of pocket bills $15k+ and counting for 2 days/standard c-section

piedmont has some practices that are the exception and not the rule when it comes to childbirth, and it cost me thousands out of pocket. 

i just received another $2,600 bill for myself and $1,800 bill for charlie for delivering my child. this brings my total 2019 oop expenses to over $23k ($750/mo in premiums--with the other $750 paid by my employer, fyi, and $7,900 max oop costs each for me and my child, in network).

expectant mothers:

*piedmont is the only local hospital that considers your child an independent person on insurance the moment they are born. this means a new deductible, co-pays, and coinsurance for that child the moment they leave your body. we are now at over $5k in oop expenses for the baby alone for standard care over 2 days (she had no problems). all other local hospitals bill the child as part of "you" for the first 30 days of life.

*ask to be told every single time--in advance of being provided non-emergency care--if the following people providing your care are in-network under your hospital or are being pulled in from an outside vendor, then check with your insurance on whether they are in your network before you see this person. this includes nurses, your doctors, anesthesiologists, pediatricians, nursery staff, specialists, and pediatricians.

*i'd suggest you request your vitals only be checked once a day, not every time a nurse changes shift. every entry into the room is a charge of multiple hundreds of dollars. change your own linens and have family bring you food, don't eat the hospital's food. request to take your own medicines and bring them. e.g. your own prescriptions, motrin (they will try to give you a drip and then will charge you $30 each time), etc. be extremely clear and demand that you give yourself those medications you brought as long as the nurse witnesses it - do not let them put them in a cup for you. basically - avoid any care that feels superfluous. they (meaning piedmont, not the medical professionals) are doing it to add to your bill.

*for any non-vital services, refuse them. e.g. some random person comes in to ask how your experience is.

*make notes or have your family make notes of every single name of every single person who walks into your room in a medical capacity, or if the baby is wheeled out, who touches them in the nursery. take notes of how many times and for how many hours, on what days, your child is in the nursery. note all services provided.

*do the same for yourself. every time your vitals are checked, bedding is changed, food is delivered, etc. (if applicable). ask for an itemized list when you leave. they only keep these records in l&d for 30 days, and your bills will come after that. 

*demand to be consulted in advance of any paperwork being filed on your behalf beyond nursing notes and notes from only doctors you have personally seen. yes, i'm serious. i got charged $351 for a doctor i had not seen "putting a nurse's notes" in another document i've never seen.

*ask before you go into labor for a list or detail of services typically provided for women giving vaginal or standard c-section birth and what the self-pay rates are so you can decide if you want to not send specific pieces through insurance or not. if you can afford it, consider self-pay regardless and submit a claim to insurance if expenses end up adding up to more than you predicted. do this with your ob as well. call your insurance company to compare. be prepared to pay your max oop costs for you and your child - unless you work with someone out of network, which will be extra.

i'd suggest you mail these logged notes to yourself in a sealed envelope the day you are discharged from the hospital, and also file copies with the billing dpt of the hospital and your insurance immediately upon release.

when you argue about this, you are told you "should have checked" whether someone was in network before you saw them. this process is all 100% legal.

i take my hat off to the doctors, nurses, and staff at medstar washington hospital center because they are slammed with wall-to-wall patients, due to the recent shut-down of providence hospital and lack of hospitals in washington, dc, yet they still maintain a courteous and friendly demeanor. 

my family member just recently spent a week in this hospital and i can honestly say, it probably saved his limb. the doctors are so knowledgeable and aggressive with their diagnosis and willing to make rapid moves to save a life. we experienced nothing but patience and understanding towards the patient, as well as the family. the doctors/surgeons made time to discuss every option and outcome with the family and it was greatly appreciated. 

now i will say that the er triage is something like a third world country war zone. i've never been, but i can only imagine. since my family member was admitted to the hospital unexpectedly from a doctor's appointment, we were told that the er would be the easiest way to be admitted. whew! well, he was admitted easily, but the triage area was flooded with people!!! people stacked on top of people, no privacy, people in the hallways, cops guarding individuals that were under arrest...just a mass chaotic mess! people yelling out, hacking, sneezing, just a big germ fest. i wanted to go home and bathe in a bathtub filled with clorox and lysol. 

i truly didn't want to leave him there because he/everyone looked so miserable. it's no way on earth anyone could get any rest in this area because it's just a big ball of confusion. he spent two days in this confusion until he could get into a room. that's how crowded this hospital is, you have to wait until a room finally becomes available before you can leave the er. i don't know how they do it, but the nurses and doctors persevere on and act as if nothing is going on. i would lose my mind if i had to deal with this chaos everyday. 

oh how i wish dc would build a new hospital or 2 to take care of the citizens of the nation's capital!!! they need it asap!!!! 

after he was placed in a room, he was able to receive the care he so desperately needed.  if i was basing my review on the er alone, it would be a 1 star review, but since i had to factor in the staff, the rapid response of the doctors and my family member's care, i had to bring that star count up. this truly is a great hospital. it's just overcrowded. i truly hope another hospital can be built in the district to alleviate some of the crowds.

my husband had an aggressive brain tumor removed october 1st with dr veronis.   this was my husband's second tumor in over a year. 
the first tumor was removed at university of miami hospital and we had no complications and he was able to leave the hospital a few days later totally fine.   
dr. veronis was going to do an awake surgery, but due to my husband's declining speech and a recently diagnosed uti, we were told it would no longer being awake surgery.  
i was concerned about potential complications, and asked what the worst case scenario would be, and was told that my husband might lose his speech and possibly his writing ability. we went ahead with the surgery.
fast forward, my husband is partially paralyzed on his right side, is incontinent, and needs a diaper for  his bowel movements.  his speech has been impacted as well. after 6 weeks of rehab, things are not getting better and we will be bringing him home for hospice (according to the neurologist/oncologist, he has 2-6 months). 
i'm angry because i feel like i should have been told the worst possible scenario (paralysis) as we may have not gone ahead with the surgery.  at least my husband would  have dignity and mobility with whatever short time was left.  
i realize that  is a medical professions problem....to operate, but sometimes it is not in the best interest of the patient if it only prolong their life for a short while.  i hope that will change.
update:  my husband passed away 2 weeks after coming home.  i'm still angry and sad.  what was the point of the surgery if the doctors knew he wouldn't have much longer to live?

if i could give zero stars, i would. last october, i came down with intense flank pain, sweating, and nausea. it was a kidney stone. i knew because it was not my first kidney stone and those symptoms are hard to forget. my employer told me to leave work early and get medical care.

i tried an urgent care first, but they refused care because they didn't have imaging equipment to diagnose a kidney stone. i asked google for the closest hospital, because i was in too much pain to drive but had no one else to drive me so i needed to get there as soon as possible.

i checked in to ahmc emergency room at 12:30pm but was not attended to (other than a urine test) until 3:00pm despite being in so much pain that i was writhing and rocking, and had short/ragged breaths. and yes, i had taken pain relievers... 4 excedrin migraine, which did absolutely nothing for my pain.

once i got into a bed at 3:00pm, where i sat without treatment or fluids for another hour. finally, at 4:00pm, i was given toradol which relieved my pain for about 30 minutes, and 1 liter of saline. then, at 4:30pm, the doctor came to chat with me for about 30 seconds and tell me he thinks i'm an alcoholic because i have pancreatitis (a pathology which can also happen if you're in extreme duress, which i had been for 5 hours) and that he's holding me overnight.

i'm not in the habit of disobeying doctors' orders, so i allowed this and informed my employer immediately. no one on the hospital staff would tell me approximately how long i would be hospitalized, only that i would be going upstairs.

well, upstairs was even worse. i didn't get there until 6:15pm (nearly 2 hours after any pain relief had long-since disappeared), and an hour passed before i was even 'checked in'. around 10pm i was finally given pain medication, but they didn't bother to ask me what medications i respond to, just asked if i had any 'tolerance issues' (code for, "are you a drug addict"). well no, i'm not, but i am an advocate for myself when it comes to pain management and morphine, which they gave me, only causes chest pain and severe anxiety.

i immediately expressed this after the nurse gave me the morphine, because i felt the familiar symptoms, and he said, "oh, well give it some time."

i suffered for 6 more hours without seeing another person's face, although i could hear them talking just outside my room and ignoring my moaning/crying from the pain. the next time someone checked on me, it was 4am. i begged for something different, even the toradol that i was given downstairs because it worked. the nurse said he'd have to check with the doctor on call. i didn't see him again for hours and when he did come back he said the doctor refused the toradol because it's "bad for the kidney," all the while i've been given just 2l of fluid for the past 18 hours. hey, idiots, kidney stones don't spontaneously pass. you have to flush them with fluid.

i finally did get a norco at 10:30am, which meant that about 18 hours passed while i was in 11/10 levels of pain and completely unable to sleep or focus on anything else to take my mind off of the pain... and, once again, listening to nurses talk about other patients while they were right outside my door and had to have heard my cries. furthermore, they would not allow me to take any of my regular medications, which meant 1) no anxiety medication, 2) no sleep medication, and 3) no depression medication when i was still there the next morning.

i begged to be discharged, because they were doing nothing to treat my pain or the cause of my pain. and it still took until 5:30pm (seven hours after the norco) for me to actually be discharged so that i could drink water and pass the stone, which i did in a walgreens bathroom while waiting for the azo and diuretics they had prescribed.

a couple of months later, i got a bill that stated my insurance (which was a 10% coinsurance, mind you) covered all but $900. the original bill was over $18,000. there were fees on the list that looked completely fraudulent, like a $700 charge to assess pulmonary function. unless that was how much my pulse-ox cost, there is no reason i should have a charge for pulmonary assessment. and my 2 liters of saline? $298.

so there you have it -- 30 hours of my life wasted on lack of treatment, only to receive a $900 bill.

since this incident led to me losing my job because my boss felt like i had taken a "vacation" without warning, i didn't have the energy to fight the bill. i just paid it. but you should do anything you can to avoid this hospital like it's the actual plague. walk, take the bus or a taxi, or pay a random stranger to take you to another hospital because all you'll get here is people ignoring you and then asking for ungodly amounts of money for it.

recently, i had a scary incident at home and called 911.  the wonderful paramedics were able to address it at home but were very forceful about my going to hosp to get checked out.  i told one of them i wanted to go to to suburban because that's my doc's hospital, but since i live so close to sg, they said that would be impossible.  i was told in the past by a much more assertive woman i know that if you push it, they will comply.  but i didn't.

the er nurses were incredible - angels. the docs were very nice and seemed knowledgeable.  they could have let me go home, but decided that i should stay overnight to be on the safe side.  i refused some meds-a shot to the gut. whaaaaaaaat?  no.  it was about 2 am at the time.  i could have walked out, but my husband and the docs, i decided, were right.  that's when things went downhill. 

the room i was assigned to was right next to nursing station.  so very noisy.  it was literally freezing in there.  not enough blankets to be comfortable.  the nurses were lovely but they kept coming in and out instead of doing what they intended to do the first time.  then they'd burst in, throw on that damned stark white overhead light and ask 25 questions that required cogent responses.  problem with this and probably most all hospitals is that cya and $ hold precedence over patients' health.  this is the *hospital policy*, not the employees' faults, but they lose good people because of it.  

finally a doc came in, said he would have let me go last night and kind of muttered about the fact that 2 short procedures would/could be done before i left.  but no one came to do them.  i waited for hours.  finally i found my nurse and said, "i'm leaving and will take responsibility for not having the procedures.  made an appt w/my doc and he'd take care of it. true, i did make the appt and he said he could do one of the procedures. he felt the other was not necessary.  

she summoned the the way overworked "hospitalist," who said i couldn't leave w/out the procedures.  she didn't mention the magic exit, which is to sign a release stating i didn't comply w/medical directives or whatever.  i said i "need to get out of here."  patients were ill all around me, coughing like they had the worst pneumonias, whooping coughs, etc.  i thought hospitals were very concerned with people catching infections while there and wanted them outta there asap, also $$$. i was going crazy.  finally had the 2 procedures.  then the waiting till i was told of the results and hopefully, released.  i tried to find my nurse, over and over and over.  finally found her and she said i'd have to sign the release. i said, "hey that's fine but *i* complied, i did the 2 tests. you guys haven't held up your side of the bargain...i should have had the results hours ago!"

she said the hospitalist had to sign the release! omg. she finally got ahold of her.  the woman looked like someone had dragged her behind their car.  she's young, very smart and competent, but they are killing her! i actually felt sorry for her, everyone was calling, approaching her, pulling at her.  that is *just* inhumane.  these cheap arse hospitals lining ceo's pockets with money and understaffing to keep it that way should be thrown in jail.....for life.  she was very nice, pulled up my results, signed my forms and i was so outta there!!!!!!  i could have cried, i was so frustrated and needed to get out of that place. 

this was disorganization at its worst.  the nurses were, overall, incredible.  but no matter how good you are, you can't do this job alone or be pressed this hard and retain your quality and/or your attitude!  i totally get that. 

at the *very* most, in the am, i should have had the two tests (15 min at most), gotten my results immediately and been sent on my way.  if they had needed the bed, magically, i prob wouldn't have *needed* the tests anymore. 

this place needs to get their act together and treat their employees right.  hire more people and get your procedures in place.  i realize there are  priorities among patient care, but a hospital or any health care facility, had to have have enough committed, serious people so that you can keep the process moving efficiently.

my doctor at kaiser vallejo is awesome. i've seen her for 15 years. she referred me to bariatrics back in 2005 because i was very challenged losing weight and was at 320 pounds. i went to the kaiser bariatric program in richmond ca, and yes, they make the patient go through all kinds of psychological tests and all kinds of classes so we can make an informed decision about whether or not to have weight-loss surgery. here's my warning for anyone thinking about having radical weight loss surgery. they'll teach you about not being able to take nsaids, drink alcohol, eat more than 5g of sugar, no time-release or extended-release medications, etc. the problem: you don't know what is yet to come. i developed osteoarthritis years later. what is the treatment for osteoarthritis? nsaids. unless you have ever had osteoarthritis, you don't have any clue how painful your life is going to be. the only pain-relieving alternative (legal and permitted by kaiser) is narcotic. percocet works really well on osteoarthritis pain. but it wears off after 3.5-4 hours. that means on really bad days you take 6 of them. a 30-day supply is 180 pills. 

kaiser used to provide 200, so there was always extra and refills were about every 4.5-5 weeks. then the government's war on opioids kicked in, and that overshadows patient needs. if someone is in pain, and has no other options for pain control, too bad so sad. sucks to be you. now kaiser limits to 90 tablets for 30 days. they wear off after 3 1/2 hours so that means more than half of the day is spent in pain. and there is no other option. i've complained all the way up the chain at kaiser to no avail. there is not another option and no fix. my recommendation to anyone considering bariatric surgery is fine out before you proceed what your options are if, 15-20 years down the road you've got arthritis that has you in pain most of the time.

all of that said this kaiser is awesome. i just wish they recognize that some patients are in real pain and are falling through the cracks and they need to find a way to address it.

have been coming to this medical center for over twenty years. as recently as last week, i did not feel good, and had symptoms synonymous to a heart condition with shortness of breath. historically, and with family history, i had a genuine concern and checked into the emergency room. my vitals were taken shortly thereafter, but after that, i waited nearly 4 hours before i was admitted, not happy, zero star!

the emergency room was crowded with patients and severely under staffed. fortunate to be physically fit but even athletes can suffer heart related issues, and i didn't want to take a chance. 
i checked in on a friday early afternoon and needed  medical treatments, tests and procedures and ended up staying for a week. that week was probably one of the worse experiences i had to endure with relentless injections, to administer medications and or draw blood for more lab work. i felt as though my blood was being sold, with the multiple amounts of blood taken from me. my arm was bruised where injection needle poked me. also, for nearly 6 days, i was feverish, as high as 104 and was freezing, yet was not allowed to have anything more than a bed sheet...i could have contracted pneumonia as a result.  i was freezing, dehydrated and desperately lacked rest and sleep...all of which added to my illness.

the nurses were attentive and seemed genuinely caring and they deserve a 5 star. the nurses seem to be more aware of department schedules and special units. most of the doctors that checked on me seemed to be clueless, promising me one treatment and no being able to deliver, due to schedule conflicts and just pure ignorance of the medical facility's political processes. in my observation, most of my attending  doctors looked to be recent graduates and lacked systematical training. also, lots of these doctors seemed to have been imported other countries and continents and lacked communication skills, some barely spoke english. did cedars compromise patient care with cheaper quasi doctors from other countries to lower their overhead salaries? i had better dialogue with the nurses who all spoke english clearly.  many of the treatments i received were administered by nurse practitioners, who were all very efficient and respectful and again deserve 5 stars. 

cedars-sinai is regarded as among the best medical facilities in south california for having almost any complex procedures not offered by many hospitals. many celebrities often come here for medical attention. although i am sure the staff are instructed and trained to maintain patient privacy, i am not convinced lots of the star struck staff adhere to those rules. i am not a celebrity, but i insisted my personal information remain private and insisted on mostly female staff as much as possible and was accommodated 85% of the time.
despite my request for privacy in a private room, i had no privacy, with constant gawkers of male staff coming into my room, pretending to do something to take a peek. i had a sheet over my head to mitigate that bothersome parade of gawkers, so unnecessary and very annoying. i didn't even have the energy to scream them out of my 'private room.'

this last weekend was not my first or last time at this medical facility but hope that any future visit will be much improved, the overall rating is more deserving of a sad pathetic 2 star...with as much funding cedars-sinai received from generous donors, room for improvement with better quality trained doctors, staffing is desperately needed, so patients receive care asap and not have to wait a long suffering 4 hours, which is unacceptable.

dr. kosari is a terrible, careless, incompetent surgeon. do not trust him. i've made that mistake twice, so i'm not sure which of us is the bigger idiot. i've tried to summarize my experience with him below, but happy to describe in more detail through message for those considering a surgery with dr. kosari.

in 2013, i started to develop an umbilical hernia just above my belly button. it was never that noticeable, but in the spring of 2019, it had grown just enough to always be noticeable to me. i was referred to dr. kosari. i thought that the reputation of cedars-sinai would hold, but i was wrong.

in the examination, dr. kosari was friendly, but clearly rushed. he let me know he only had about 10 minutes. i explained i'd had the hernia for a few years and, while seated, he asked me to lift my shirt, briefly touched the belly button (literally for less than a second) where it was visible and that was it for the exam. he said he'd recommend doing the surgery with stitches, not mesh. knowing nothing about the difference, i trusted his judgment.

the day of the surgery, i was a bit tense as this was my first surgery. i was also concerned he had not adequately inspected the hernia (and he had not ordered any type of ultrasound). i waited for about 2 hours and then they took me in to prepare me. when i saw dr. kosari before the surgery, i explicitly asked him, "so you are going to be able to fix not only the part below the belly button, but also above it, right?" dr. kosari responded, "yes, don't worry. once we're in, we'll be able to check it all to see what we're dealing with."

i woke up after the procedure and went home. i had the surgery on friday, sep 13. i removed the bandage (which was covering the belly button and surrounding area) and showered on sunday, sep 15. by monday, i felt the hernia above my belly button exactly as before the surgery. panic immediately struck. i called cedars-sinai and was able to tell dr. kosari's nurse i felt a bulge exactly like the hernia, and she told me to just come in for my checkup in 2 weeks for dr. kosari to examine it.

when dr. kosari examined me, he tried to say there was nothing wrong, or that it was something else (like a result from the surgery or a problem with "skin" being "detached"). i told him, "no...i am 100% sure this is the same hernia i've had...it feels exactly the same." he told me to come back in 4 more weeks after the recovery period "to see if it's still there." that really aggravated me, i left the appointment knowing i still had the hernia, but he wouldn't acknowledge it.

at the next appointment, he acknowledged i still had a hernia, but never acknowledged it was because of his carelessness. compared to the first surgery, he was pushing much more strongly for not operating again. i think it's because it would make him look bad to have to repeat the exact same surgery, but i scheduled a follow up surgery for dec 3 anyway to get it dealt with once and for all (had already pretty much met my out of pocket max, so thought why not - and couldn't get in to ucla before the end of the calendar year - book ahead!).

on dec 3, i had the second surgery, and this time we did an ultrasound before the surgery. again, he did not recommend mesh, just a single stitch he said. this time, i didn't notice the hernia for a few weeks, but could definitely feel a slight bump, which i thought might be the stitch or something. now, just over 6 weeks since the second surgery, i still have the hernia. i can feel it exactly the same as i used to.

after one surgery, i'd expect a hernia to be fixed, at least for a few years before it might recur. after two surgeries, i would really expect a hernia to be fixed. now, after spending thousands of dollars, taking months off from the gym for two separate recoveries, and still having the problem that was supposed to be fixed, i'm so filled with anger and frustration about this "doctor." he is careless, negligent, or uses poor judgment in making choices for his patients' care. 

please, do not select this doctor. i will be seeing dr. chen from ucla instead....happy to compare my experience after my third hernia surgery for the same hernia. in my last check-up after the second surgery, dr. kosari told me, "if it comes back let me know and we can go back in there with the mesh." to myself, i thought this moron will never touch my body again. don't let yourself become another one of his mistakes. i will forever regret it, but hopefully i can get a successful surgery from ucla and eventually put this behind me. but i'm sure i will continue to live with the nightmares about the hernia problems that i've had ever since the first surgery was unsuccessful, i hope you can learn from my pain and experience to avoid the same experience with this terrible doctor. cedars-sinai should not allow this man to be operating under their name.

as they say, "fool me once, shame on you, fool me twice shame on me." he won't be fooling me a third time.

i am an rn with a master's degree and was also an aprn for 10 years. having been a healthcare provider for many years, i am saddened to write a negative review of a hospital.

i was sent to the er by my primary doctor's office. when i arrived at ascension seton hays county er in kyle, the waiting room was not overly crowded, and it was evident some of the people were not patients but family members of patients. i was optimistic for a quick visit. 

i made sure to confirm that not only the hospital but all related to my care would be in-network with my medical insurance. i knew seton was in-network, but i did not want anyone involved in my care who was not in-network. i know seton has not been very good about this in the past.

after i was triaged, i was told to sit again in the waiting room. since i had to use the bathroom, i was directed to collect a sample. sitting in the waiting room holding a container of urine on my lap felt incredibly awkward. in fact, i was so embarrassed that for part of the time, i felt compelled to put it in my handbag. 

when i was called to the back, i was led to a stretcher in the hallway. that is where i remained throughout my care from assessment through treatment through discharge. 

way back in nursing school, i was taught to always introduce myself by name and role to each patient, for instance, "hi. i'm sandra, and i will be your nurse today." i consistently did this throughout my career regardless if i was wearing a name tag or id, and i strongly believe that every provider in healthcare should do the same, from technicians to nurses to physicians. during my visit at seton's er, some staff did introduce themselves to me such as ashley (the triage nurse) and the er doctor. however, there were others involved with my care who did not. 

from my place in the hallway, i had a front row seat to everything. the patient in the room next to my stretcher was obviously dying. family members sat next to and stood near my stretcher. i felt like i was intruding on their grief. as a caring person, i wanted to reach out and provide support, but i kept quiet since i really should not have even been aware of what was going on with them and the patient.

at another point, i heard a commotion going on behind the head of my stretcher. it was not particularly loud, but i heard security involved, and i felt frightened. i did not dare turn around to see what was going on, but i did watch as security walked a man in handcuffs down the hallway. i hope i had not been in any danger.

when my iv was removed, a band-aid was placed in my antecubital space where the iv had been located. shortly after, i noticed my arm felt wet and cold. i looked down and saw that i was bleeding profusely and that my beloved sweater was getting soaked with bright red. a nurse (well, i assume she was a nurse; she never introduced herself) brought over a bottle of hydrogen peroxide and a stack of gauze to remove the blood. she started the process pouring the peroxide on my sweater, but it would take a while to remove such a quantity of blood, so she left me with the supplies to continue working on it myself. finally, i got my sweater mostly clean, but i was left very wet and cold.

it was taking a long time to get final lab results, and then i learned that the lab had lost my specimen! how does that even happen? is the lab not in the same building? a mishap like that does not instill confidence. hopefully the lab does not also accidentally mix up samples or misread them or misreport them.

i spent almost 4 hours at ascension hays seton to have a few simple tests done (no imaging) and a medication administered (a push, not a slow drip). it was not like the er was chaotic. in fact, i watched many staff sitting behind the desk for much of my time there.

close to the time of my discharge, i was approached to sign a consent to treatment. it seemed quite late to be asking for that. i was feeling so frustrated by that point that i signed the various forms without reading anything. i was also told that with insurance i owed $*** just for walking into the er (the amount did not include tests, etc.). she wanted to collect money right there on the spot. i handed over my credit card, thinking this trip to was the biggest waste of money and time i could have imagined. i dread thinking about the remainder of my bill still yet to come.

every staff member i encountered was nice, and i appreciate them. still, i would not recommend ascension seton hays er in kyle. obviously, i strive and wish for good health and hope i never have to go to an emergency room again. however, if i do, i will first check into my other options before heading to seton.

as soon as he left, it was like the green berets of rns came in and things were in motion extremely quickly. there was also a high school student from gpnhs in there?? they must have given me the happy juice before she came in because in retrospect that's freaking weird. anyway, very little chatting and then i was on my way to the or. 

there were tons of people in there which i assume is normal. but that hs student was in there too! (oh, what gpf money can buy!) i barely remember anything past moving to the operating table. it would have been nice for my surgeon to stop in again before i was asleep.

when i woke up in recovery all i could hear was a nurse telling me to breathe deeply, and telling me that my surgeon couldn't find my husband. nice wake-up call but whatever. i couldn't breathe well because i was in a lot of pain. her only response was "that's normal, you just had major surgery". whuh?? i get that i had to get the anesthesia out but the total disregard for my pain and comfort was really frustrating. it's also so bright in there. i had to ask for a towel to put over my eyes. that nurse and another were concerned about my oxygen levels at one point, but i literally couldn't breathe deeply. i was really sad that they couldn't give me any tips/tricks for taking better breaths, but just kept snapping at me.

i then went to my private recovery room. my husband came back (he was at home, which is just around the corner). from this point on i was still in a lot of pain and kept telling the nurse there. her only solution was to "go get the doctor so he could admit for pain management". giant eye roll. maybe you could just be patient and give me an hour to 1. wake up and 2. let the meds kick in? so rude. surgeon came in again to follow up on one issue that came up, but he was in a huge rush again. not that i needed him to stay by my bedside but it was literally like "went well. put ice on the incision. bye." 

the initial recovery room nurse went on break evidently, so then a nurse named nan (pretty sure. i was a little high still, lol) came in. she was great. finally someone who helped me breathe normally, and recommended that i sit up in a chair to help with both the breathing and the pain. nan was so wonderful. she took my vitals one more time.

then i decided just to get my butt home so i didn't have to deal with the rush there anymore. the initial recovery nurse came back and once my husband helped me
get dressed, she was stripping the bed before i even got all the way into the wheelchair. nice exit. see ya.

like i said, a rollercoaster. like anyplace i'm sure there are good and bad employees. at times this really felt like a factory, though, which was disheartening. i'm thankful all the people who took care of me did so, though, and i trust the doctors here immensely. the experience just leaves some desires.

let's start with the g6 sensors themselves and the fact that since october 2018, the average amount of time a sensor lasts on my son is a paltry 4.33 days (only 8 sensors since then have lasted the full 10 days!)i've tried everything to get them to last longer, from listening to all the (often contradictory) advice that support reps give - one person tells me to pinch the skin at the attachment site before attaching, another person tells me not to do that. we've tried hydrating him more, that didn't work. someone even told us to try not to calibrate if we can avoid it, because that throws the sensor into a tailspin and eventually it will fail. more on what a messy situation that is later. what i had been doing about all these sensor failures up until a few months ago, was when i got a chance, i would call in with the information i captured in a spreadsheet (lot #, attachment date, attachment location on the body, whether or not i applied an overpatch, the date it was removed and the reason for removal) and the support specialist would take the total number of days i should have gotten out of x sensors, subtract out the number of days i did get, and round up to the next number of sensors, and 3-5 days later, i'd have the sensors replaced. for instance, if 7 sensors lasted 34 days, the support rep would say "7 sensors should last 70 days. they lasted 34, so we owe you 36 days, which you can get out of 36/10 = 3.6 or 4 sensors." it wasn't ideal, but as a very busy person, being able to call in when i could to get sensors replaced was the only thing that made all these sensor failures halfway tolerable.

then, they instituted a policy that they would replace only 3 sensors per call, and the rest would have to be approved, adding a new dimension to the dysfunction that is the g6. customer support reps continually assure me that i am not the only one having these issues, so why in the hell would they institute a policy like this when there are so many problems with the g6? now instead of waiting to do this when i can, i have to call every time one fails? i just don't have the time to do that! the same person who first apprised me of this policy  told me i could send email instead of calling. great! but then i get a return email asking me to take more time i don't have to fill out a patient request form (the description field of which accepts 126 characters max!), and then after i've done that, now i have to wait an additional 2-3 business days to get a call back, and even if that happens on time (which it doesn't always) over the course of all of this, 2 more sensors have failed. they've created a bottleneck with this 3-sensor-limit policy. most of the time, they approve the 3 sensors and leave any remaining sensors in limbo waiting for "approval."  i had needed 6 sensors, the rep who i was on the phone with sent 3, and told me i'd have to wait for the other 3 to be approved. after not hearing back for about 3 weeks, i called in and the rep just sent the sensors. so what was the fucking point of that? they didn't even need to get approved! they just added a layer to make it more difficult for me. i patronize the company because it is supposed to provide working devices, and when they don't work, to have them replaced swiftly, not to create impediments for every type of problem i could have and then not even stick to those policies. dexcom should be creating solutions, not problems.

finally, dexcom g6 has this habit of asking me to recalibrate every 15 minutes if the fingerstick calibration value is too far off from the sensor reading. on christmas night at about 11:35pm the sensor reported my son's bg was low, and before i go throwing glucose down his throat, i did a fingerstick. the fingerstick came back with 93, and when i calibrated, it told me to recalibrate after 11:50pm. it's almost midnight and i'd really like to go to sleep, but i figured i'd play along. at about midnight, i fingerstick again,106. i put that in the dexcom app. now it wants me to calibrate after 12:05am." so then i do it again, and it says calibrate at 12:20m.  i don't have time to jerk this thing off.  dexcom openly admits it is for information purposes and may not be accurate and also admit that the fingerstick is the more accurate indicator of what the blood sugar actually is. then why on earth do i have to keep doing this for hours even at 1 in the morning when i want to sleep because the fingerstick doesn't agree with dexcom!? when i put in the fingerstick value it should adjust to that, period. this calibrate over and over again is pure horseshit and it goes against everything we know about which is the accurate one and which is to be used for information purposes! now support would say "after the 2nd or 3rd calibration, you should just replace the sensor." but you can see why i want every sensor to last as long as possible, because every sensor failure is is another addition to the boondoggle that is the sensor replacement process.

the mount sinai hospital provides a miserable patient experience
mount sinai has many fine doctors and many wonderful nurses.  i am not here commenting on the medical care that may be received at this hospital.  rather i am talking about the hospital culture and approach to the patients - which is execrable.  

my 97 year old mother, alert and bright, was taken there with a broken hip two weeks after an emergency heart surgery.  she sat up all night in an overcrowded, overworked and understaffed er (see ny post of december 9, 2019: https://nypost.com/2019/12/09/mount-sinai-hospitals-emergency-department-is-a-war-zone-workers-say/ ) before being loaded on a gurney and taken to an overflow facility.  in the course of her transfer all of her clothing, shoes, jewelry, outer- and under-wear disappeared.  the following day, when i first learned of the loss, i notified security and the patient ombudsman and provided an itemized list of missing items.  those two offices supposedly conducted an investigation.  they found no sign of the goods but would reveal nothing of their efforts nor share any of their report.  i have no basis to know whether any investigation was conducted or any report generated.

after 6 weeks of a run-around within the hospital proper i wrote to the general counsel who referred me to an outside law firm.  the outside law firm allegedly referred the matter to be investigated - and had me wait another month before telling me, more than 9 weeks after the loss, that they would offer us pennies on the dollar to go away.  

while in the hospital, my mother was served a diet erroneously prescribed by the hospital nutritionist.  it took daily efforts, with the help of doctors, nurses and the nutritionist, for more than ten days, to have that corrected - during which time my mother was largely unable to eat the food provided to her.  i brought in food on a regular basis to be sure she had adequate nutrition and a hot meal she could stomach.  

due to repeated surgical delays, poor communication, aggressive medication, and general abuse by the hospital my mother, who arrived at the hospital bright and optimistic, left it feeling depressed and defeated.  

my family has recorded additional examples of incompetence and broken promises from the hospital during this stay, but this may be sufficient to bring home the point that the patient experience at mount sinai is one of insouciance and disrespect.  

finally i would note that my mother's late husband was a surgeon at mount sinai, an emeritus professor in their medical school, their historian and archivist, a recognized author and historical contributor to various medical disciplines - and she, known to be his widow, was still treated in this uncaring manner. (she does not deserve better treatment for that relationship, but it might have been offered.)  based on direct, repeated and anecdotal experience, the description of the mount sinai er in the post article and my mother's experience were neither isolated nor unique.  

if you have a choice of hospital facility, and you care for the mental state and dignity of your "patient", i would strongly suggest nyu, cornell or another hospital would provide a far preferable environment and a comparable medical experience.

tl;dr:  mt sinai's er doctors refused to provide me with care for excruciating pain and as a result i nearly lost my life to sepsis. months after this experience, i finally have the presence of mind to post this review as a warning to others.

i visited this er at the urging of my doctor, who is affiliated with mt sinai. he feared that i might have an infection in my spine and wanted me to have some imaging and blood tests done because they didn't feel it could wait until the next week. my partner drove me to the er and we were seen very quickly - it was very quiet and we could only see 3 or 4 patients with relatively mild issues. we met with a resident, erik sherman, who did not listen to my situation at all, saying flatly that there wasn't much they could do for back pain. we asked again for an mri and the resident said "well, mris are very expensive and you might be waiting for hours," and my partner replied that our insurance would absolutely cover it and that we were fine with waiting as long as needed. 

my partner asked to speak with the attending, bess storch, and we again explained the entire situation and serious concerns our doctor had that led him to us to the er. dr. storch repeated that they were unable to do imaging and that i should follow up next week because this was "an in-office case."when she left the room, my husband called my doctor's answering service, yelled for the attending to come back, and he handed her his phone and begged her to speak with him. my doctor confirmed everything we had told them, and asked for the same tests we had asked for. begrudgingly, the attending allowed me to have an x-ray only.

we waited for a few hours for the x-ray and by the time they wheeled me back (i couldn't walk) a nurse came and said they had already discharged me. we waited for another 2 + hours and then we were handed the imaging report, which showed that i had a compression fracture on one of the vertebrae in my upper back. they said it was common and not a concern so we just left, completely demoralized and just happy to be out of there after more than 8 hours. a few days later, i was taken to another er by ambulance and was diagnosed with sepsis caused by a severe infection and an abscess that was pushing against my spine so hard that it caused a fracture. i needed emergency surgery and i spent months recovering inpatient. if mt sinai's er doctors had just listened to us and run tests, we might have known about the abscess sooner and my life would not have been put in extreme jeopardy. i nearly died. you should all be ashamed to call yourselves doctors.

this is a review for their labor and delivery part of the hospital.

i'm currently writing this in the recovery room, having just delivered my second baby (first one with el camino, first was with ucsf in the city). i just wanted to use this moment to rave about my experience this time around compared to ucsf.

from triage to l&d to recovery, all the doctors and nurses here are by far the most experienced, kind, knowledgeable and kind people i have ever met. due to covid i never got a chance to do a hospital tour, so i had no idea what to expect when i checked in 2 nights ago after laboring for 24h at home.

at triage i was greeted by nurse melissa, who checked me and i hadn't progressed enough to be admitted. instead of just sending me home, she asked me to walk the hallway for 1h to see if it'll speed things up. and it did, i went from 3cm to 5cm during that hour and was admitted right after.

the rest of the nursing team were all super pleasant, knowledgeable and explained every little thing to me without me having to ask. there's a really positive energy and rapport between the nurses so it carries through the whole bedside manner. my iv drip at ucsf last time was a traumatic experience, they couldn't find my vein and blood kept spurting everywhere. this time at el camino, they had a nurse who specialized in iv insertion and she did it painlessly and perfectly in one to without any blood. 

i knew i wanted an epidural this time, and instead of dictating to me when i should get it, they told me to tell them whenever i wanted it. i decided to walk for another hour before asking for the epidural. now let's talk a bit about the epidural. i had dr. k (forget the full name) and he was so good. no pain, super calm, and the meds took effect almost immediately. with ucsf i was in so much pain and the injection didn't even work the first time, i had to wait 2h for the anesthesiologist to come back to up my dosage. this time, the dosage was perfect because i had no pain but eventually i could feel the pressure as i was nearing 10cm. i could move my legs and could feel the pressure of contractions so my pushing was super effective. i'm told this is the perfect dosage and that the doctor is really good.

now onto the pushing phase. at ucsf (since it's a teaching hospital) there were 10+ people in the room while i was pushing. some were helping while others were just spectating. this time, i had one nurse stay with me the whole time helping me push, and once it got to a certain point she called my ob and she came and took it to the finish line. hardly tore, got 2 stitches and no hemorrhages. i tore second degree and hemorrhaged pretty badly with my first.

once baby was here, they moved us to the mother & baby section. since the epidural wore off rather quickly i was able to pee way faster than with my first, and the nurses in recovery were all super nice and accommodating. i also had a fabulous lactation consultant help me with breastfeeding, who really gave me the most helpful pointers that i never got with my first. when i was at ucsf with my first, i had a lot of pain in latching and the lc there told me that nothing was wrong and a "little" pain is normal. basically made me feel like a wuss. turned out my firstborn had a tongue tie and lip tie but i didn't get that diagnosed til she was already 3mo. of course by then my breastfeeding journey was already a hot mess and did not go well at all. the lc at el camino (stacey was her name) took her time to teach me how to latch and basically said that proper breastfeeding should never hurt. after 30min of training i was able to find a good latch and now my baby is breastfeeding really well. night and day.

anyways, i just wanted to take the time to give credit to an incredible group of staff. it's seriously night and day to my experience at ucsf and i wouldn't have known unless i had something to compare against. 

thank you for such a pleasant birthing experience. i never knew i would ever use "pleasant" to describe labor and delivery.

insanely overpriced lab services. our family doctor used to work with quest, and is now associated with the el camino health network. this means they send lab tests through el camino hospital labs, and then bill separately. a few standard tests that should have cost under $200 were billed as over $4000, then reduced due to a negotiated in-network rate with blue cross to "only" a third. i went to my insurance website and looked up the prices for the exact same procedures. quest is not even the lowest cost provider, yet their cost would have been less than a tenth of the final bill from el camino. so their prices are marked up 30-fold.
even if you have maxed out your entire deductible your copay alone will be higher than going to a different lab service. if this is your first procedure of the year, rest assured lab services at el camino are going to put a significant dent into your deductible. 
how can you avoid this? ask your doctor which lab they are using for blood work. if he does not know, ask the nurse who would take your blood, where they will send the blood. if they are sending it to el camino, you can insist that you want to use an independent lab service. you can then go with referral/instructions from your doctor to quest or a similar lab service. it will save you on average over $100 per test.

if i'm paying for an epidural, then i better have it. she also got mad at me for crying when it was time to push and angrily questioned "why are you crying!?" what the...? giving birth to my first child was very exciting and i was extremely overwhelmed with emotion, and she thinks she can question me for tears of joy? i'm pretty sure that crying is normal during child birth. she then rolled her eyes with disgust and lectured me saying "i'm gonna tell it to you straight, but if you waste your energy on crying, you are going to spend an hour pushing! we can get this baby out in 15 minutes or you can waste your energy, and it will take an hour!" at one point she made me feel so bad for not getting the baby out quicker that i started apologising to her. talk about mind games. she had no right to make me feel guilty for taking longer than she wanted. i spent in total about an hour pushing, which i later found out is not an unreasonable amount of time. after the baby was born she huffed out of the room. no congratulations, just a scowl. unfortunately all her scolding triggered anxiety attacks which later snowballed into postpartum depression and other health complications. i had to see a shrink about her trauma. also for about a week after the delivery, my body ached all over and my lungs hurt from pushing too hard. looking back, i now know that i hurt my lungs pushing too hard. but then i had no clue what was wrong with me. i went to the er, and they ordered a ct scan, but then the doctor later told me that a blood clot was very unlikely being that i'm already on thinners and it was likely just soreness from the delivery. so they made me endure an expensive diagnostic test that exposes me to cancer causing radiation even though i'm already on blood thinners and it was very unlikely to be a blood clot?! beaware and demand to see all lab results and question everything as er doctors like dr. reyes are not trustworthy!!!   as a 3rd generation "redlander" that was born at redlands community hospital and who has defended it many times when i have heard people say. "if you need more than a band-aid don't go there,"  i am saddened to write this review but feel it is important so that others are not victim to having to pay double co-payments when they should have never been released but they trusted what the doctor told them.  the only reason i give it 2 stars is because the nurses and staff at the er were kind and helpful.  i learned the hard way to challenge what a doctor tells you and never leave until you physically see your lab reports, as dr. reyes convinced my family and i that i should be fine and even though i still had many of the symptoms and pain that i came in with. but dr. reyes told me "as long as i was not vomiting i would be ok."  i should have never been discharged with lab levels 8 times the normal range (the doctor never told me the number - not sure even if she had the complete report when she released me).  it should have been quite obvious to an er physician that the lab results grossly indicated a severe, aggressive, and active infection when in reality my parents and i were not told anything besides, "you have some form of stomach issue and your labs seem a little wonky," by dr. sonia-maria reyes.  great medical vocab don't you think?   eight times the normal level  is anything besides a "little wonky" especially after telling her that my symptoms had gotten progressively worse over the previous 48 hour period and i was worried as i was leaving for college in less than12 days.  not being a doctor, and never being told just how "wonky" my lab results really were, i unfortunately trusted the doctor and followed the doctor's directive to go home not knowing any other option and not realizing i could object and that she was just "practicing" medicine.  if i had not been discharged and would have been admitted and started on iv antibiotics that day, i am certain that i would not have had to suffer another two days at home hoping that what the er doctor prescribed was going to eventually help, when in fact it did not and i was back at the er on 2 days later, to then be admitted and be charged yet again!  it was my primary doctor's office that called my mom to check on me on monday and was appalled that i was sent home with the lab results that they saw.  my primary called and talked to the head of the er and i was told to immediately return to rch to be admitted and stayed for 2  1/2 days on multiple iv doses of antibiotics.   i had no problem having to pay my $575 co-pay from when i was admitted but then i received another bill for my first er co-pay another $250 which would not have had to be paid if i was admitted the first day as i should have been.  
 i sent my bill and concern to rch's appeals process and never heard back so i resubmitted it.  i actually received a letter this time but it stated that i still have to pay it because "both my parents and i were made aware of discharge plan."  it would have never happened if i or my parents were made aware of my actual lab results so again i urge everyone to challenge everything the doctor tells you, have them show you proof and do your research before you let them kick you out - i now understand why medicare now institutes the "hospital readmission reduction program" that does not pay the hospital for discharges that had a readmission within 30 days.  maybe all insurance companies should look into that for all age patients to protect them too!  i hope rch will reconsider and reimburse me for the additional $250 that i should not have had to pay, but regardless, i will never just believe an er doctor again - i will sit in that bed until i physically see all of the results and take time to look things up as they are many reports online about similar lab results that i had and even some that were less than mine where patients were not discharged!  you have been warned - be your own advocate for sure!!!
